Weak-LαL^{\alpha} Noise, Strong Guarantees:
Gradient Clipping under Affine Heavy Tails

Alyona Nekrasova1   Makar Sidorov2   Savelii Chezhegov3 Alexander Gasnikov4   Margarita Preobrazhenskaia2 Igor Preobrazhensky2   Eduard Gorbunov5 1Independent researcher   2Yaroslavl State University 3Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence 4Innopolis University   5Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
October 20, 2026
Abstract

Gradient clipping is a key tool for obtaining high-probability convergence guarantees for stochastic first-order methods under heavy-tailed noise. Existing analyses typically assume a bounded central moment of order α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2], which excludes distributions with tails of order u−αu^{-\alpha} at the critical exponent. In this paper, we consider smooth convex optimization under affine heavy-tailed noise, whose scale may grow with the gradient norm. We derive high-probability convergence guarantees for clipped SGD (Clip-SGD) and its accelerated variant Clip-SSTM under a weak-LαL^{\alpha} tail condition, which is strictly weaker than the corresponding moment bound. For 1<α<21<\alpha<2, the clipping bounds have the same powers of the clipping level as in the moment case, and both methods attain the additive stochastic rate K−(α−1)/αK^{-(\alpha-1)/\alpha}. The gradient-dependent noise contributes a faster-decaying term of order K−2(α−1)/αK^{-2(\alpha-1)/\alpha}, up to logarithmic factors. At α=2\alpha=2, we characterize the additional logarithmic factor on the Lorentz scale and establish its necessity for the additive error at fixed confidence. We also analyze Clip-SGD with prescribed clipping levels and derive finite-horizon guarantees for reaching a neighborhood determined by the clipping bias. For additive noise, matching lower bounds show that this neighborhood is unavoidable, up to constants and the natural error cap. Numerical experiments with Pareto noise illustrate the theoretical results.

1 Introduction

Gradient clipping rescales a stochastic gradient whenever its norm exceeds a prescribed level λ\lambda. It is a standard tool for stabilizing the training of machine learning models. It was introduced to handle exploding gradients in recurrent neural networks (Pascanu et al.,, 2013) and is now used in large-scale training pipelines, including GPT-3 (Brown et al.,, 2020) and LLaMA (Touvron et al.,, 2023). It is also a basic component of differentially private SGD (Abadi et al.,, 2016). One explanation for its usefulness is that stochastic gradient noise can be heavy-tailed, as observed in deep learning and language-model training (Şimşekli et al.,, 2019; Zhang et al., 2020b, ). Moreover, SGD iterates can have heavy-tailed stationary distributions even for light-tailed data (Gürbüzbalaban et al.,, 2021). Under a bounded central moment of order α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2], clipped SGD (Clip-SGD) converges with high probability and logarithmic dependence on the inverse failure probability, whereas SGD without clipping may fail when the variance is infinite (Zhang et al., 2020b, ; Gorbunov et al.,, 2020; Sadiev et al.,, 2023). Section 2 discusses extensions of these results.

Two limitations of much of the existing high-probability theory motivate this work. First, the moment assumption 𝔼​‖g⁡(x,ξ)−∇f​(x)‖α≤σα\mathbb{E}\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|^{\alpha}\leq\sigma^{\alpha} is stronger than the tail control used in our analysis. Pareto distributions and non-Gaussian α\alpha-stable distributions with α∈(1,2)\alpha\in(1,2) have tails of order u−αu^{-\alpha} but an infinite α\alpha-th moment; the latter have been proposed as models of stochastic gradient noise in deep learning (Şimşekli et al.,, 2019). A moment theorem therefore applies only at a smaller exponent, with a slower polynomial rate when that exponent is fixed. The weak-LαL^{\alpha} (Marcinkiewicz) condition ℙ{∥g(x,ξ)−∇f(x)∥>u}≤σαu−α\mathbb{P}\{\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|>u\}\leq\sigma^{\alpha}u^{-\alpha} controls the tail directly.

Second, many high-probability analyses tune the clipping level to the noise parameters and the horizon and assume a uniform noise scale on the relevant region. Practical implementations often use a prescribed constant level, and the noise scale may vary with the gradient. Although prior work addresses some of these features separately (Section 2), their combination under a local weak-tail condition motivates the following question:

What do clipped methods guarantee under a pure tail condition on the noise, with a noise scale that grows with the gradient norm, and with a clipping level chosen by the user?

In this paper, we address this question for Clip-SGD and its accelerated variant Clip-SSTM.

Our contributions.

We analyze Clip-SGD and Clip-SSTM under affine moment and weak-LαL^{\alpha} noise conditions, which allow the noise scale to depend on the gradient norm. Table 1 compares the guarantees for horizon-dependent tuning with prior results. Table 3 summarizes the guarantees and lower bounds for prescribed clipping levels. Our contributions are as follows.

  • ∙\bullet

    Clipping under tail conditions. We bound the clipping bias and the second moment of the clipped error under a weak-LαL^{\alpha} tail condition. The bounds have the same powers of the clipping level as in the moment case, with an unavoidable logarithmic factor at α=2\alpha=2 (Lemma 4.1).

  • ∙\bullet

    New high-probability results for Clip-SGD and Clip-SSTM. With horizon-dependent tuning, both methods attain high-probability rates with explicit constants (Theorems 5.1 and 5.2). In the nontrivial stochastic regime, the additive term is optimal in KK, σ0\sigma_{0}, and RR; the corresponding confidence dependence is optimal under the moment condition and under the weak-tail condition for α<2\alpha<2 (Theorem I.18 and Propositions H.2 and H.3). At the weak-L2L^{2} endpoint, the additive term contains the necessary factor ln⁡(e​K)\sqrt{\ln(eK)} at fixed confidence (Corollary I.19). The gradient-dependent noise contributes a faster-decaying term. For Clip-SSTM, this follows from a weighted bound on the true gradients; we do not establish optimality of the multiplicative term.

  • ∙\bullet

    Prescribed clipping levels. For sufficiently large prescribed clipping levels, we bound the error of the averaged iterate by a clipping-bias neighborhood plus terms that vanish with the horizon (Theorem 5.3). For arbitrary positive clipping levels, we obtain a best-iterate guarantee under additive or sufficiently small multiplicative noise; the weak-tail version requires α<2\alpha<2 (Theorem 5.4). Additive-noise lower bounds show that the neighborhood is unavoidable up to α\alpha-dependent constants and truncation at L​R2LR^{2} (Theorem 5.5). For additive noise, a clipping level proportional to (K+1)1/α(K+1)^{1/\alpha}, held constant within each run, recovers the rate K−(α−1)/αK^{-(\alpha-1)/\alpha} up to logarithmic factors.

  • ∙\bullet

    Numerical experiments. In Section 6 and Appendix J, we illustrate the derived results in numerical experiments with Pareto noise.

2 Related Work

We discuss the closely related works below and defer a more detailed overview to Appendix B.

High-probability bounds under heavy-tailed noise.

High-probability guarantees with logarithmic dependence on the inverse failure probability were first obtained for clipped and truncated stochastic methods under bounded variance by Nazin et al., (2019) and Gorbunov et al., (2020). Sadiev et al., (2023) extended the analysis to bounded central moments of order α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2]. For smooth convex problems, they derive the rate O~(LR2/K+σRK−(α−1)/α)\widetilde{O}(LR^{2}/K+\sigma RK^{-(\alpha-1)/\alpha}) for Clip-SGD and its accelerated counterpart for Clip-SSTM. These are the closest constant-scale results: Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 recover them when σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0 and the moment condition holds (Table 1).

The weak-LpL^{p} condition itself is used by El Bakkali et al., (2026) for zeroth-order non-convex optimization under global sample-wise smoothness and a constant noise scale. Their methods clip scalar directional derivatives and use mini-batches or a momentum scheme with a warm-start batch. We consider first-order methods for convex problems with one oracle call per iteration, under a local tail condition whose scale may grow with the gradient norm. Our assumption requires neither symmetry nor a density. Appendix B discusses the full range of bounded-moment results, structural noise assumptions, and methods without clipping, including the accelerated convex method of He et al., (2025).

Affine noise, fixed clipping levels, and lower bounds.

Affine variance is classical in the analysis of SGD (Bottou et al.,, 2018; Gower et al.,, 2019; Khaled and Richtárik,, 2023). Most high-probability analyses under heavy-tailed noise use a constant scale on the relevant region; state-dependent finite-variance bounds appear in Tsai et al., (2022); Das et al., (2024), and affine moment bounds are considered in the concurrent work of Lobanov et al., (2026).

For a fixed clipping level, Koloskova et al., (2023) characterize the clipping bias and derive tight in-expectation guarantees under bounded variance. Khah et al., (2026) obtain high-probability bounds for the best iterate with an arbitrary clipping level under a bounded moment assumption. Table 3 compares their regime λ>4​L​R\lambda>4LR. We extend prescribed-level guarantees to affine weak-LαL^{\alpha} noise and derive matching additive-noise lower bounds, distinguishing averaged and best iterates.

Stochastic convex lower bounds go back to Nemirovski and Yudin, (1983). Vural et al., (2022) establish the optimal heavy-tailed rate K−(α−1)/αK^{-(\alpha-1)/\alpha}, and Liu, 2026a () derive high-probability lower bounds for non-smooth convex problems. Our lower bounds concern smooth unconstrained problems and capture the confidence dependence and the additional logarithmic factors at the weak-L2L^{2} endpoint.

Concurrent work.

Lobanov et al., (2026) analyze a restarted accelerated method with clipping and projection under (H0,H1)(H_{0},H_{1})-smoothness (Alimisis et al.,, 2026) and a moment bound combining additive, gradient-dependent, and function-gap-dependent noise. Their method uses one sample per iteration. For LL-smooth objectives and no function-gap-dependent term, their convex complexity has the same polynomial dependence as Theorem 5.2, including the dependence on σ1\sigma_{1}, whose optimality remains open in both works.

Their analysis covers generalized smoothness, strong convexity, and noise decaying with the function gap. We analyze Clip-SGD and Clip-SSTM without restarts or projections under a tail condition on a ball, including the weak-L2L^{2} endpoint with infinite variance, and study prescribed clipping levels. Appendix B gives the precise assumptions, complexity comparison, and relation between the lower bounds.

3 Problem Setup

We consider the following stochastic optimization problem and assumptions.

Notation.

We use the standard notation: ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle denotes the standard inner product in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| is the induced Euclidean norm, Br​(x):={y∈ℝd:‖y−x‖≤r}B_{r}(x):=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\|y-x\|\leq r\} is the ball with center at xx and radius rr, (a)+:=max⁡{a,0}(a)_{+}:=\max\{a,0\}, and 𝟏A\mathbf{1}_{A} is the indicator of an event AA. For a σ\sigma-algebra 𝒢\mathcal{G}, 𝔼[⋅∣𝒢]\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid\mathcal{G}] denotes the conditional expectation w.r.t. 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Problem.

We consider the stochastic optimization problem

minx∈ℝd⁡f⁡(x),\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(x), (1)

where f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is Borel measurable and accessible only through the stochastic oracle specified below. We assume that a minimizer x∗x^{*} exists and write f∗:=f⁡(x∗)f^{*}:=f(x^{*}). Following Sadiev et al., (2023), we impose the smoothness, convexity, and noise assumptions only on a ball around a minimizer. Given R≥‖x0−x∗‖>0R\geq\|x^{0}-x^{*}\|>0, we use Q=B2​R​(x∗)Q=B_{2R}(x^{*}) for Clip-SGD and Q=B3​R​(x∗)Q=B_{3R}(x^{*}) for Clip-SSTM. The analysis shows that the relevant iterates remain in these balls with high probability. No smoothness or convexity is required outside QQ.

Assumptions on ff.

We start with the standard assumptions on the objective function.

3.1Local LL-smoothness.

We assume that ff is LL-smooth on QQ, i.e., ‖∇f​(x)−∇f​(y)‖≤L​‖x−y‖\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\| for all x,y∈Qx,y\in Q.

3.2Gradient bound.

We assume that ‖∇f​(x)‖2≤2​L​(f⁡(x)−f∗)\|\nabla f(x)\|^{2}\leq 2L\left(f(x)-f^{*}\right) for all x∈Qx\in Q.

3.3Local convexity.

We assume that ff is convex on QQ, i.e., f⁡(y)≥f⁡(x)+⟨∇f​(x),y−x⟩f(y)\geq f(x)+\left\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\right\rangle for all x,y∈Qx,y\in Q.

If ff is convex and LL-smooth on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, then Assumptions 3.1–3.3 hold for any RR. Here these properties are required only on QQ, which contains the relevant iterates with high probability. Assumption 3.2 follows from Assumptions 3.1 and 3.3, since QQ is a ball centered at x∗x^{*} (Lemma E.1). We state it separately to simplify the comparison with Sadiev et al., (2023).

Stochastic oracle.

Let 𝒢0:=σ⁡(x0)\mathcal{G}_{0}:=\sigma(x^{0}) and 𝒢k:=σ⁡(x0,ξ0,…,ξk−1)\mathcal{G}_{k}:=\sigma(x^{0},\xi^{0},\dots,\xi^{k-1}) for k≥1k\geq 1. The oracle is a jointly measurable, finite vector field g⁡(x,ξ)∈ℝdg(x,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfying 𝔼ξ​[g⁡(x,ξ)]=∇f​(x)\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[g(x,\xi)]=\nabla f(x) for all x∈Qx\in Q. It need not be the gradient of a random function; expected-loss minimization with g=∇fξg=\nabla f_{\xi} is a special case. At iteration kk, the method samples ξk∼𝒟\xi^{k}\sim\mathcal{D} independently of 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k} and queries the oracle at a 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}-measurable point. The noise assumptions hold only on QQ; outside QQ, the oracle is an arbitrary finite jointly measurable extension. Appendix E explains why these pointwise assumptions apply to adaptive queries and why the extension does not enter the bounds. We consider two affine noise models, whose scale may grow with the gradient norm.

3.4Affine moment condition.

We assume that there exist σ0,σ1≥0\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1}\geq 0 and α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2] such that for all x∈Qx\in Q we have 𝔼ξ​[g⁡(x,ξ)]=∇f​(x)\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[g(x,\xi)]=\nabla f(x) and

𝔼ξ​‖g⁡(x,ξ)−∇f​(x)‖α≤σ0α+σ1α​‖∇f​(x)‖α.\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|^{\alpha}\leq\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}\|\nabla f(x)\|^{\alpha}. (2)
3.5Affine weak-LαL^{\alpha} (Marcinkiewicz) condition.

We assume that there exist σ0,σ1≥0\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1}\geq 0 and α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2] such that for all x∈Qx\in Q we have 𝔼ξ​[g⁡(x,ξ)]=∇f​(x)\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[g(x,\xi)]=\nabla f(x) and, for all u>0u>0,

ℙ{∥g(x,ξ)−∇f(x)∥>u}≤σ0α+σ1α​‖∇f​(x)‖αuα.\mathbb{P}\left\{\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|>u\right\}\leq\frac{\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}\|\nabla f(x)\|^{\alpha}}{u^{\alpha}}. (3)

Condition (3) restricts only the tail of the noise. Equivalently, ‖‖g⁡(x,ξ)−∇f​(x)‖‖Lα,∞α≤σ0α+σ1α​‖∇f​(x)‖α\left\lVert\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|\right\rVert_{L^{\alpha,\infty}}^{\alpha}\leq\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}\|\nabla f(x)\|^{\alpha}, where ‖⋅‖Lα,∞\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{L^{\alpha,\infty}} denotes the weak-LαL^{\alpha} quasi-norm. For α>1\alpha>1, this quasi-norm is equivalent to the norm of the Marcinkiewicz space MαM_{\alpha}, which is a classical rearrangement-invariant Banach space (Kreĭn et al.,, 1982; Bennett and Sharpley,, 1988); see Appendix C for the details. By Markov’s inequality, Assumption 3.4 implies Assumption 3.5 with the same σ0,σ1,α\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1},\alpha, but the converse implication does not hold at the same exponent: weak-LαL^{\alpha} noise may have infinite α\alpha-th moment and, for α=2\alpha=2, infinite variance (see the example in Section 3). When σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0, Assumption 3.4 recovers the standard heavy-tailed noise assumption (Zhang et al., 2020b, ; Sadiev et al.,, 2023).

Example: Pareto noise at the critical index.

Weak-LαL^{\alpha} noise can have an infinite α\alpha-th moment. For example, non-Gaussian symmetric α\alpha-stable distributions with α∈(1,2)\alpha\in(1,2), proposed as models of stochastic gradient noise in deep learning (Şimşekli et al.,, 2019), have tails ℙ{|Y|>u}∼cαu−α\mathbb{P}\{|Y|>u\}\sim c_{\alpha}u^{-\alpha} as u→∞u\to\infty (Samorodnitsky and Taqqu,, 1994). For a concrete example, let σ>0\sigma>0, α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2], and ξ=σ​ε​𝖱\xi=\sigma\varepsilon\mathsf{R}, where ε\varepsilon is an independent Rademacher sign and ℙ{𝖱>u}=min{1,u−α}\mathbb{P}\{\mathsf{R}>u\}=\min\{1,u^{-\alpha}\}. Then 𝔼​ξ=0\mathbb{E}\xi=0, ‖ξ‖Lα,∞=σ\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{L^{\alpha,\infty}}=\sigma, and 𝔼​|ξ|α=∞\mathbb{E}|\xi|^{\alpha}=\infty, while 𝔼​|ξ|q=σq​α/(α−q)\mathbb{E}|\xi|^{q}=\sigma^{q}\alpha/(\alpha-q) for 0<q<α0<q<\alpha (Proposition C.7). Thus, the moment condition applies only at a smaller exponent, whereas the weak-tail condition holds at the critical exponent with the exact scale. The Pareto tail bound is attained for u≥σu\geq\sigma, and a dd-dimensional version is ξ=σ​𝖱​U\xi=\sigma\mathsf{R}U, where UU is independent and uniform on the unit sphere. Our experiments use symmetric or centered asymmetric Pareto noise in scalar or one-directional form, with an affine scale S⁡(x)S(x).

Considered methods.

For λ>0\lambda>0, the clipping operator is defined as follows: clip​(v,λ):=min⁡{1,λ/‖v‖}​v\texttt{clip}(v,\lambda):=\min\{1,\lambda/\|v\|\}\,v for v≠0v\neq 0 and clip​(0,λ):=0\texttt{clip}(0,\lambda):=0. We study the convergence of clipped SGD (Clip-SGD, Algorithm 1) in terms of its averaged iterate x¯K:=1K+1​∑k=0Kxk\bar{x}^{K}:=\frac{1}{K+1}\sum_{k=0}^{K}x^{k}, and of its accelerated variant Clip-SSTM, which we introduce in Section 5.1.

4 Clipping under Affine Heavy-Tailed Noise

The key technical ingredient of the high-probability analysis of clipped methods is a lemma bounding the bias and the variance of the clipped stochastic gradient. In this section, we generalize Lemma 5.1 from Sadiev et al., (2023) to the setting of this paper, i.e., to the noise satisfying either the affine weak-LαL^{\alpha} condition or the affine α\alpha-th moment condition. For brevity, we denote A⁡(x):=σ0α+σ1α​‖x‖αA(x):=\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}\|x\|^{\alpha}.

4.1Clipping under affine heavy-tailed noise.

Let α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2], λ>0\lambda>0, and let XX be a random vector in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} such that 𝔼​X=x\mathbb{E}X=x, ‖x‖≤λ/2\|x\|\leq\lambda/2, and either (a) ℙ{∥X−x∥>u}≤A(x)u−α\mathbb{P}\{\|X-x\|>u\}\leq A(x)u^{-\alpha} for all u>0u>0, or (b) 𝔼​‖X−x‖α≤A⁡(x)\mathbb{E}\|X-x\|^{\alpha}\leq A(x). Let X~:=clip​(X,λ)\widetilde{X}:=\texttt{clip}(X,\lambda). Then ‖X~−𝔼​X~‖≤2​λ\|\widetilde{X}-\mathbb{E}\widetilde{X}\|\leq 2\lambda almost surely, 𝔼​‖X~−𝔼​X~‖2≤𝔼​‖X~−x‖2\mathbb{E}\|\widetilde{X}-\mathbb{E}\widetilde{X}\|^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}\|\widetilde{X}-x\|^{2}, and

The full statement (Theorem F.1) gives the bound 2​R2/(γ⁡(K+1))2R^{2}/(\gamma(K+1)) for every admissible stepsize γ≤γ∗\gamma\leq\gamma_{*}. The horizon logarithm in ℓ\ell comes from a union bound. A maximal inequality replaces ℓ\ell by ln⁡(4/β)\ln(4/\beta) under the moment condition and under the weak-tail condition for α<2\alpha<2 with v=vα​(∞)v=v_{\alpha}(\infty) (Theorem I.18; see also Nguyen et al.,, 2023). Proposition H.3 establishes optimality of this confidence dependence for the additive stochastic term. The same replacement applies to Clip-SSTM. Discussion.

Under Assumption 3.4 with σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0, the stochastic term σ0RK−(α−1)/α\sigma_{0}R\,K^{-(\alpha-1)/\alpha} cannot be improved, up to the logarithmic factor and the constant, by any algorithm making K+1K+1 oracle calls, even if one asks for the guarantee with constant probability: Proposition H.2 (Appendix H) provides a convex LL-smooth instance on ℝ\mathbb{R} with ‖x0−x∗‖=R\|x^{0}-x^{*}\|=R and 𝔼​|ζ|α≤σ0α\mathbb{E}|\zeta|^{\alpha}\leq\sigma_{0}^{\alpha} such that the error is at least 14min{σ0R(K+1)−(α−1)/α,2LR2}\frac{1}{4}\min\{\sigma_{0}R(K+1)^{-(\alpha-1)/\alpha},2LR^{2}\} with probability at least 1/41/4; the proof relies on the two-point argument of Bubeck et al., (2013). Since Assumption 3.4 implies Assumption 3.5 with the same parameters, the same lower bound holds for the larger class as well. That is, for α<2\alpha<2 the weaker assumption costs nothing in the rate and affects only the α\alpha-dependent constants. Next, the terms depending on σ1\sigma_{1} decay faster in KK than the σ0\sigma_{0}-term; for α=2\alpha=2 under Assumption 3.4, the last term in (7) is of the order σ12​L​R2​ℓ/K\sigma_{1}^{2}LR^{2}\ell/K, which together with the first term recovers the well-known (1+σ12)​L​R2/K(1+\sigma_{1}^{2})LR^{2}/K scaling under affine variance.

The endpoint α=2\alpha=2 and the Pareto example.

Under Assumption 3.5 with α=2\alpha=2, the noise may have infinite variance at every point (Section 3), meaning that the analyses relying on the bounded second moment are not applicable. Nevertheless, Theorem 5.1 gives the rate of the finite-variance case, max⁡{L​R2​ℓK,σ0​R​c​ℓK,c​σ12​L​R2​ℓK}\max\{\frac{LR^{2}\ell}{K},\sigma_{0}R\sqrt{\frac{c\ell}{K}},\frac{c\sigma_{1}^{2}LR^{2}\ell}{K}\} up to absolute constants, with the logarithmic factor c=c2​(ΛK)=O⁡(ln⁡(K+1)+ln⁡(1+Λ2​2​L​R))c=c_{2}(\Lambda_{K})=O(\ln(K+1)+\ln(1+\Lambda_{2\sqrt{2}LR})); the same holds for Clip-SSTM (Theorem 5.2). A logarithmic factor is unavoidable both in the clipping lemma (Remark D.3) and in the rate: at a fixed confidence level, no algorithm using KK stochastic gradients can avoid the factor ln⁡(e​K)\sqrt{\ln(eK)} in the additive term over the weak-L2L^{2} class, and, more generally, the factor [ln⁡(e​K)]1/2−1/s[\ln(eK)]^{1/2-1/s} on the Lorentz scale L2,sL^{2,s} (Proposition I.16 in Appendix I.8; this order is attained, see Corollary I.19). Therefore, for the Pareto example from Section 3, the weak-LαL^{\alpha} analysis gives the exponent (α−1)/α(\alpha-1)/\alpha with a KK-independent constant for α<2\alpha<2 and the finite-variance exponent 1/21/2 up to a logarithmic factor for α=2\alpha=2, whereas the moment-based analysis can be applied only with some q<αq<\alpha and σ0=(αα−q)1/q​σ\sigma_{0}=(\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-q})^{1/q}\sigma: a fixed qq leads to the slower exponent (q−1)/q(q-1)/q, and choosing q→αq\to\alpha with the growth of the horizon recovers the exponent (α−1)/α(\alpha-1)/\alpha only up to a factor of the order (ln⁡K)1/α(\ln K)^{1/\alpha} (see Corollary F.3 in Appendix F).

The oracle complexity implied by (8) is given in Table 1 (see Corollary I.2). When σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0, bound (8) has the same powers of KK as the moment-based results of Gorbunov et al., (2020) (α=2\alpha=2) and Sadiev et al., (2023), but it holds for the larger class Lα,∞L^{\alpha,\infty}; at α=2\alpha=2 under Assumption 3.5, it gives the finite-variance rates for the noise whose variance may be infinite, with the logarithmic factor vv, which Proposition I.13 (Appendix I.8) refines on the Lorentz scale L2,sL^{2,s}.

Role of the direct Lorentz analysis.

For fixed L,R,σ0>0L,R,\sigma_{0}>0, additive noise, and fixed confidence, the moment-embedding route in Corollary I.19 improves the direct Lorentz bound by a factor ln⁡(e​K)\sqrt{\ln(eK)}. Its additive term matches the lower bound in Proposition I.16 in the stochastic regime. The direct analysis remains useful because it gives explicit finite-horizon parameters under the original affine Lorentz condition. Appendix I.8 gives the detailed comparison. Neither result establishes optimality of the multiplicative term or of the joint dependence on KK and a vanishing failure probability.

Why the affine structure is preserved.

The key idea of the proof is to bound the true gradients along the trajectory by induction via the function gap: on the induction event, the potential of SSTM gives At​(f⁡(yt)−f∗)≤32​R2A_{t}(f(y^{t})-f^{*})\leq\frac{3}{2}R^{2}, and Assumptions 3.1–3.2 turn this into ωt+1​‖∇f​(xt+1)‖≤7​R/a\omega_{t+1}\|\nabla f(x^{t+1})\|\leq 7R/\sqrt{a}, which implies ∑t<Tωt+1α​‖∇f​(xt+1)‖α≤7α​Rα​T/aα/2\sum_{t<T}\omega_{t+1}^{\alpha}\|\nabla f(x^{t+1})\|^{\alpha}\leq 7^{\alpha}R^{\alpha}T/a^{\alpha/2} (see Lemma I.5 in Appendix I.4), whereas the crude bound ‖∇f​(xt+1)‖≤2​L​R\|\nabla f(x^{t+1})\|\leq 2LR gives only Rα​Kα+1/aαR^{\alpha}K^{\alpha+1}/a^{\alpha}.

This weighted estimate preserves the gradient-dependent noise scale throughout the clipping analysis. As a result, the multiplicative contribution is bounded by σ12​L​R2​(H/K)2​r\sigma_{1}^{2}LR^{2}(H/K)^{2r}, compared with σ1​L​R2​(H/K)r\sigma_{1}LR^{2}(H/K)^{r} when the noise is bounded uniformly on QQ (Corollary I.9). This improves the bound’s dependence on KK; it does not establish optimality of the multiplicative term. Faster rates are known under additional multiplicative-noise structure (Appendix I.7).

5.2 Prescribed Clipping Levels

The clipping levels in Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 depend on the parameters of the problem and on the horizon, whereas in practice λ\lambda is a constant chosen by the user. In this section, we allow the user to prescribe λ\lambda. Theorem 5.3 bounds the error of the computable averaged iterate x¯K\bar{x}^{K} for any λ≥2​2​L​R\lambda\geq 2\sqrt{2}LR; this is a geometric condition guaranteeing that the true gradient is never clipped in B2​R​(x∗)B_{\sqrt{2}R}(x^{*}), and it involves neither β\beta nor KK (nor the noise, except for the case α=2\alpha=2 with σ1>0\sigma_{1}>0). Theorem 5.4 covers any λ>0\lambda>0 (for additive noise or for multiplicative noise below an absolute threshold; under Assumption 3.5, only for α<2\alpha<2), but it bounds the best iterate mint≤K⁡f⁡(xt)\min_{t\leq K}f(x^{t}), which cannot be selected using the gradient information only. In both results, only the clipping level is free: the stepsizes still depend on the noise and confidence parameters. Below, (b,v)(b,v) are the clipping constants from Section 5 with Λ=Λλ\Lambda=\Lambda_{\lambda} under Assumption 3.5; only bb affects the size of the neighborhood.

where εN:=48​2​c⟂​R​b¯λ\varepsilon_{N}:=48\sqrt{2}\,c_{\perp}R\,\bar{b}_{\lambda}, εM:=384​c⟂​σ1α​L​R2​min⁡{1, 96​c⟂​σ1α}\varepsilon_{M}:=384\,c_{\perp}\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}LR^{2}\min\{1,\,96\,c_{\perp}\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}\}, and 𝒱λ,K′\mathcal{V}^{\prime}_{\lambda,K} collects the terms vanishing as K→∞K\to\infty, of the orders K−1/2K^{-1/2}, K−1K^{-1} and K−2K^{-2} up to logarithmic factors, which are given explicitly in Theorem G.1.

Theorem 5.4 bounds the first time an iterate reaches the stated neighborhood, so its stepsize need not decrease as 1/K1/K. The tuning still depends on the horizon. The guarantee concerns the best iterate in objective value, as in Khah et al., (2026); selecting an output with the same guarantee requires function values or an additional validation procedure.

For σ1>0\sigma_{1}>0, the bound has the additional term εM=O⁡(σ12​α​L​R2)\varepsilon_{M}=O(\sigma_{1}^{2\alpha}LR^{2}), which does not decrease in λ\lambda. The key new ingredient of the proof is a clipping lemma for arbitrary clipping levels (Lemma G.2): when ‖∇f​(x)‖>λ/2\|\nabla f(x)\|>\lambda/2 and ‖∇f​(x)‖≳σ0\|\nabla f(x)\|\gtrsim\sigma_{0}, the mean clipped gradient has a component of size at least min⁡{‖∇f​(x)‖,λ}/6\min\{\|\nabla f(x)\|,\lambda\}/6 along ∇f​(x)\nabla f(x), provided that σ1≤σ¯1\sigma_{1}\leq\bar{\sigma}_{1}, and an orthogonal component bounded by a quantity of order λ​A​(∇f​(x))/max⁡{‖∇f​(x)‖,λ}α\lambda A(\nabla f(x))/\max\{\|\nabla f(x)\|,\lambda\}^{\alpha}. The analysis of Khah et al., (2026) compares the mean clipped gradient with clip​(∇f​(x),λ/2)\texttt{clip}(\nabla f(x),\lambda/2). It covers arbitrary λ>0\lambda>0, with additional terms involving ζλ:=max⁡{0,2​L​R−λ/2}\zeta_{\lambda}:=\max\{0,2LR-\lambda/2\} when λ<4​L​R\lambda<4LR. Table 3 compares the regime λ>4​L​R\lambda>4LR, where ζλ=0\zeta_{\lambda}=0. We also notice that some restriction on σ1\sigma_{1} is necessary for small clipping levels: for the multiplicative oracle of Faw et al., (2023) (σ0=0\sigma_{0}=0, σ1≤9\sigma_{1}\leq 9) on f⁡(x)=L2​x2f(x)=\frac{L}{2}x^{2}, Clip-SGD with any fixed λ>0\lambda>0 and γk≤1/L\gamma_{k}\leq 1/L started from x0=λ/Lx^{0}=\lambda/L stays at distance ≥λ/(2​L)\geq\lambda/(2L) from x∗x^{*} forever with probability ≥2/3\geq 2/3 (Proposition H.6).

5.3 Lower Bounds for a Fixed Clipping Level

The next result shows that the additive-noise neighborhood from Theorem 5.4, and hence the first part of 𝒩λ\mathcal{N}_{\lambda} in Theorem 5.3, cannot be improved for any λ>0\lambda>0, up to the factors depending on α\alpha and the trivial level L​R2LR^{2}. More precisely, for any λ>0\lambda>0 we construct a one-dimensional problem with additive noise such that Clip-SGD with λk≡λ\lambda_{k}\equiv\lambda and any deterministic stepsizes does not approach the solution.

Let L,R,σ0,λ>0L,R,\sigma_{0},\lambda>0, α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2], and let ελ:=148⋅4α​min⁡{R​b¯λ,L​R2}\varepsilon_{\lambda}:=\frac{1}{48\cdot 4^{\alpha}}\min\{R\bar{b}_{\lambda},LR^{2}\} with b¯λ=min⁡{σ0,σ0α/λα−1}\bar{b}_{\lambda}=\min\{\sigma_{0},\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}/\lambda^{\alpha-1}\} from (11). Then there exist a convex LL-smooth function f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} with minimizer x∗=0x^{*}=0, a point x0x^{0} with |x0−x∗|=R|x^{0}-x^{*}|=R, and an oracle g⁡(x,ξ)=f′​(x)+ζg(x,\xi)=f^{\prime}(x)+\zeta with 𝔼​ζ=0\mathbb{E}\zeta=0 and 𝔼​|ζ|α≤σ0α\mathbb{E}|\zeta|^{\alpha}\leq\sigma_{0}^{\alpha} (i.e., Assumptions 3.1–3.5 hold on ℝ\mathbb{R} with σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0) such that Clip-SGD with λk≡λ\lambda_{k}\equiv\lambda and any deterministic stepsizes γk>0\gamma_{k}>0 satisfies 𝔼​f​(x^)−f∗≥ελ\mathbb{E}f(\hat{x})-f^{*}\geq\varepsilon_{\lambda} for every iterate x^=xk\hat{x}=x^{k} and every convex combination x^\hat{x} of x0,…,xKx^{0},\dots,x^{K} with deterministic weights, in particular, for x¯K\bar{x}^{K}; moreover, 𝔼​f​(xk)−f∗\mathbb{E}f(x^{k})-f^{*} grows linearly in ∑j<kγj\sum_{j<k}\gamma_{j}. If γk≤R16​λ\gamma_{k}\leq\frac{R}{16\lambda} for all kk, then, with probability at least 3/43/4, f⁡(xk)−f∗≥ελ/2f(x^{k})-f^{*}\geq\varepsilon_{\lambda}/2 and f⁡(x¯k)−f∗≥ελ/2f(\bar{x}^{k})-f^{*}\geq\varepsilon_{\lambda}/2 for all k≥0k\geq 0. Comparison with the upper bounds.

Let σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0, and assume that the conditions of the upper-bound result under consideration are satisfied. Let b¯λ=min⁡{σ0,σ0α/λα−1}\bar{b}_{\lambda}=\min\{\sigma_{0},\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}/\lambda^{\alpha-1}\}. Theorem 5.5 gives the lower bound ελ=(48⋅4α)−1​min⁡{R​b¯λ,L​R2}\varepsilon_{\lambda}=(48\cdot 4^{\alpha})^{-1}\min\{R\bar{b}_{\lambda},LR^{2}\} in expectation for every iterate and every deterministic average under arbitrary deterministic stepsizes; if γk≤R/(16​λ)\gamma_{k}\leq R/(16\lambda), it also gives the lower bound ελ/2\varepsilon_{\lambda}/2 with probability at least 3/43/4, simultaneously for all iterates and their averages. This restriction on the stepsizes is satisfied by the tuning γ≤R/(40​λ​ℓ)\gamma\leq R/(40\lambda\ell) used in the upper bounds. In the regime R​b¯λ≤L​R2R\bar{b}_{\lambda}\leq LR^{2}, the best-iterate neighborhood εN=48​2​c⟂​R​b¯λ\varepsilon_{N}=48\sqrt{2}\,c_{\perp}R\bar{b}_{\lambda} from Theorem 5.4, at the confidence level β<1/4\beta<1/4, matches this high-probability lower bound up to the factor 2⋅482​2⋅4α​c⟂2\cdot 48^{2}\sqrt{2}\cdot 4^{\alpha}c_{\perp}, which depends only on α\alpha. For the averaged iterate, we impose λ≥2​2​L​R\lambda\geq 2\sqrt{2}LR and the nontrivial-regime condition R​σ0α/λα−1≤L​R2R\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}/\lambda^{\alpha-1}\leq LR^{2}. These conditions imply σ0<λ\sigma_{0}<\lambda, and, therefore, the neighborhood 120​b​R​σ0α/λα−1120\,bR\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}/\lambda^{\alpha-1} from Theorem 5.3 matches the same lower bound up to the factor 11520⋅4α​b11520\cdot 4^{\alpha}b; see Table 3 in Appendix H. Note that these comparisons concern only the neighborhoods: the lower bound does not depend on KK and does not match the terms vanishing with the horizon.

The proof (Appendix H) relies on a Huber function whose slope is smaller than the clipping bias of a two-point noise, so that the mean clipped field has the same sign everywhere and pushes the iterates away from x∗x^{*}. Consequently, a uniform guarantee in expectation 𝔼​f​(x¯K)−f∗≤ε\mathbb{E}f(\bar{x}^{K})-f^{*}\leq\varepsilon over the class of problems with additive noise and parameters (L,R,σ0,α)(L,R,\sigma_{0},\alpha), where ε<min⁡{R​σ0,L​R2}/(48⋅4α)\varepsilon<\min\{R\sigma_{0},LR^{2}\}/(48\cdot 4^{\alpha}), requires λ≥σ0​(σ0​R/(48⋅4α​ε))1/(α−1)\lambda\geq\sigma_{0}(\sigma_{0}R/(48\cdot 4^{\alpha}\varepsilon))^{1/(\alpha-1)} regardless of the deterministic stepsizes; on the other hand, for the high-probability criterion with λ=σ0​(120​b​σ0​R/ε)1/(α−1)\lambda=\sigma_{0}(120b\,\sigma_{0}R/\varepsilon)^{1/(\alpha-1)} (if this value is at least 2​2​L​R2\sqrt{2}LR), the neighborhood from Theorem 5.3 equals ε\varepsilon, and the bound becomes at most ε\varepsilon after K=Oα​(v​ℓ​(σ0​R/ε)α/(α−1))K=O_{\alpha}(v\ell(\sigma_{0}R/\varepsilon)^{\alpha/(\alpha-1)}) iterations, which is the complexity from Table 1. Moreover, the expected error of the last iterate also grows linearly in the total stepsize, which makes the scale of the bias condition from Theorem 5.3 necessary for the averaged iterate with a constant stepsize, and the bias persists even on strongly convex quadratics (see Appendix H.1).

6 Numerical Experiments

We illustrate the effect of clipping under weak-LαL^{\alpha} noise with an infinite α\alpha-th moment. On a quadratic problem with asymmetric noise, we compare the plateaus produced by prescribed clipping levels with the decreasing errors obtained using a horizon-dependent level. Appendix J reports additional experiments with symmetric noise, ridge regression, and the full theoretical parameter choices for Clip-SGD and Clip-SSTM.

Protocol.

We use α=3/2\alpha=3/2, 10241024 independent runs for each configuration, and horizons n≤106n\leq 10^{6} oracle calls, and we report the mean of f⁡(x¯n−1)−f∗f(\bar{x}^{n-1})-f^{*} together with pointwise approximate 95%95\% confidence bands; the horizon-dependent configurations are rerun for each horizon, with β=0.05\beta=0.05. The noise is built from a Pareto random variable PP with ℙ{P>t}=t−α\mathbb{P}\{P>t\}=t^{-\alpha} for t≥1t\geq 1 (so that 𝔼​P=3\mathbb{E}P=3 and 𝔼​Pα=∞\mathbb{E}P^{\alpha}=\infty): g⁡(x)=x+S⁡(x)​Zg(x)=x+S(x)Z with the centered asymmetric Z=(P−3)/2Z=(P-3)/2 and S⁡(x)=(σ0α+σ1α​|x|α)1/αS(x)=(\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}|x|^{\alpha})^{1/\alpha}. This oracle satisfies the affine weak-tail inequality with (σ0,σ1)(\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1}), and its α\alpha-th moment is infinite whenever the noise scale is non-zero.

Influence of the clipping level.

We consider the quadratic f⁡(x)=x2/2f(x)=x^{2}/2 on ℝ\mathbb{R} (L=1L=1, x∗=0x^{*}=0, x0=1x^{0}=1) with the asymmetric noise and (σ0,σ1)=(0.05,0.001)(\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1})=(0.05,0.001), and compare the constant clipping levels λ∈{0.1,0.5,1,4}\lambda\in\{0.1,0.5,1,4\} with the level λ⁡(n):=R/(40​γ∗​(n)​ℓn)\lambda(n):=R/(40\gamma_{*}(n)\ell_{n}) from Theorem 5.1, computed for each horizon nn with β=0.05\beta=0.05 and the stepsize γ∗​(n)\gamma_{*}(n) from Theorem F.1; this level grows as n1/αn^{1/\alpha} up to logarithmic factors. All variants use γ=0.05\gamma=0.05 (see Figure 1).

Figure 1 shows distinct plateaus for constant clipping levels, with smaller plateaus at larger levels. The dotted lines show objective values at zeros of the mean clipped field and provide a reference for these plateaus. With λ⁡(n)\lambda(n), the observed error continues to decrease over the tested horizons, consistently with the displayed reference slope and the heuristic n−2/3n^{-2/3} balance between squared bias and the variance of averaged clipped noise. Increasing the level reduces clipping bias while increasing the second-moment bound. All configurations use the empirical stepsize γ=0.05\gamma=0.05, so this comparison isolates the clipping level rather than testing the theorem’s full parameter prescription.

7 Conclusion

We derived high-probability guarantees for Clip-SGD and Clip-SSTM under affine weak-LαL^{\alpha} noise. For α<2\alpha<2, the tail condition preserves the polynomial rates available under a bounded α\alpha-th moment. At α=2\alpha=2, the additive term requires a logarithmic correction; our Lorentz-scale upper and lower bounds identify its optimal asymptotic order at fixed confidence and fixed positive problem parameters. The analysis also separates the additive and gradient-dependent noise contributions and gives guarantees for prescribed clipping levels. In the additive case, matching lower bounds characterize the resulting clipping-bias neighborhood up to constants and truncation at L​R2LR^{2}.

Several questions remain open. These include lower bounds for the multiplicative term, sharper guarantees for small clipping levels under multiplicative noise, and the joint dependence on the horizon and the failure probability at the endpoint.

Appendix B Extended Related Work

We expand the comparison from Section 2, distinguishing the noise assumptions, the dependence of its scale on the current point, the clipping schedule, and the type of guarantee. Our analysis concerns smooth convex problems and high-probability bounds. The non-convex, non-smooth, light-tailed, and in-expectation results below provide complementary context.

Light-tailed noise and boosting.

Logarithmic dependence on the inverse failure probability is classical under sub-Gaussian noise (Nemirovski et al.,, 2009) and extends to sub-Weibull noise, which has all moments (Li and Liu,, 2022). For strongly convex problems, Davis et al., (2021) obtain high-confidence guarantees from low-confidence solvers using robust distance estimation. Their concrete stochastic-gradient instantiations assume light tails or bounded variance, whereas the abstract reduction applies whenever suitable solvers for the regularized subproblems are available. Below, we focus on direct analyses of clipping and on alternative methods for heavy-tailed noise.

Clipped methods for convex problems under bounded moments.

Under bounded variance, Nazin et al., (2019) analyze truncated Mirror Descent, and Gorbunov et al., (2020) analyze Clip-SGD and Clip-SSTM for smooth convex and strongly convex problems. Related guarantees cover monotone and structured non-monotone variational inequalities (Gorbunov et al.,, 2022), non-smooth convex problems (Gorbunov et al., 2024a, ), and subgradient schemes (Parletta et al.,, 2024). Sadiev et al., (2023) replace bounded variance with a bounded central moment of order α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2] for smooth convex, strongly convex, and monotone variational inequality problems. We recover their smooth convex rates when σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0 (Table 1). The smooth convex analyses of Gorbunov et al., (2020); Sadiev et al., (2023) tune the clipping level to the horizon and bound the noise scale by a constant on a ball around the solution.

Nguyen et al., (2023) remove the horizon logarithm from the confidence factor for clipped Mirror Descent and its accelerated variant. Liu and Zhou, (2023) obtain a similar confidence dependence for non-smooth convex problems, together with in-expectation rates and adaptation to the initial distance. Our Theorem I.18 gives the corresponding reduction via a maximal Freedman inequality. Liu, 2026a () refine the non-smooth analysis using a generalized effective dimension and derive high-probability and in-expectation lower bounds, which we compare with ours in Section 5.

Further extensions cover composite and distributed problems and variational inequalities (Gorbunov et al., 2024b, ), distributed Clip-SGD over networks (Yang et al.,, 2026), and, in expectation, distributed methods with local updates (Lee et al.,, 2025). Clipping has also been analyzed for AdaGrad-Norm and Adam-Norm (Chezhegov et al.,, 2025), convex (L0,L1)(L_{0},L_{1})-smooth problems (El Bakkali El Kadi et al.,, 2025), weakly convex problems (Zhu et al.,, 2025), and zeroth-order non-smooth convex optimization (Kornilov et al.,, 2023). Other settings include parameter-free online learning (Zhang and Cutkosky,, 2022), differential privacy with an arbitrary clipping level (Khah et al.,, 2026), and streaming estimation (Tsai et al.,, 2022; Das et al.,, 2024). These guarantees use moment or variance bounds.

Concurrent work.

Lobanov et al., (2026) (arXiv, 27 September 2026) analyze RCSAG – a restarted clipped stochastic accelerated gradient method – for differentiable convex and strongly convex objectives under (H0,H1)(H_{0},H_{1})-smoothness, i.e., f⁡(y)≤f⁡(x)+⟨∇f​(x),y−x⟩+(H0+H1​(f⁡(x)−f∗))​‖y−x‖2f(y)\leq f(x)+\left\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\right\rangle+(H_{0}+H_{1}(f(x)-f^{*}))\|y-x\|^{2} for ‖y−x‖≤rH\|y-x\|\leq r_{H} (LL-smoothness corresponds to H1=0H_{1}=0 with L=2​H0L=2H_{0}), and a conditionally unbiased oracle satisfying, in our notation, 𝔼​‖g⁡(x,ξ)−∇f​(x)‖α≤σ0α+σ1α​‖∇f​(x)‖α+σ2α​(f⁡(x)−f∗)α/2\mathbb{E}\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|^{\alpha}\leq\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}\|\nabla f(x)\|^{\alpha}+\sigma_{2}^{\alpha}(f(x)-f^{*})^{\alpha/2}, α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2], at every query point (their Assumption 3). This is a moment condition: for σ2=0\sigma_{2}=0, it coincides with Assumption 3.4 imposed on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and otherwise it has an additional term decaying with the function gap.

In the convex case, the method runs a logarithmic number of phases starting from an upper bound on f⁡(x0)−f∗f(x^{0})-f^{*}; each phase starts from a point whose gap is at most the current bound, runs an accelerated scheme of Nesterov type with one clipped sample per iteration, whose auxiliary sequence is projected onto a bounded convex set Q∋x0,x∗Q\ni x^{0},x^{*} of diameter DD, with the clipping level and the number of iterations chosen according to this bound, DD, and the noise and smoothness parameters, and halves the bound with high probability (their Theorem 8, which relies on a maximal Freedman inequality for a stopped potential).

The total number of oracle calls (their Theorem 9) is O~​(D​H0/ε+H1​D​JH+(σ0​D/ε)α/(α−1)+(σ1​D​[H0/ε+H1​JH(α−1)/α])α/(α−1)+(σ2​D/ε)α/(α−1)+S)\widetilde{O}\big(D\sqrt{H_{0}/\varepsilon}+\sqrt{H_{1}}DJ_{H}+(\sigma_{0}D/\varepsilon)^{\alpha/(\alpha-1)}+(\sigma_{1}D[\sqrt{H_{0}/\varepsilon}+\sqrt{H_{1}}J_{H}^{(\alpha-1)/\alpha}])^{\alpha/(\alpha-1)}+(\sigma_{2}D/\sqrt{\varepsilon})^{\alpha/(\alpha-1)}+S\big), where S=⌈log2⁡(Δ0/ε)⌉S=\lceil\log_{2}(\Delta_{0}/\varepsilon)\rceil for an initial bound Δ0≥f⁡(x0)−f∗\Delta_{0}\geq f(x^{0})-f^{*} and 0<ε≤Δ00<\varepsilon\leq\Delta_{0}, and JH≤SJ_{H}\leq S counts the phases with H1​2−s​Δ0>H0H_{1}2^{-s}\Delta_{0}>H_{0}; for H1=0H_{1}=0 and σ2=0\sigma_{2}=0, this has the same polynomial dependence, up to constants and logarithmic factors, as the complexity of Theorem 5.2 in Table 1, with D=2​RD=2R in place of RR (their Appendix G.1 takes Q=BR​(x0)Q=B_{R}(x^{0}) when RR is known), including the dependence on σ1\sigma_{1}, whose optimality is open in both works.

Under strong convexity (their Theorem 10), the method uses shrinking balls centered at the restart points, and only the σ0\sigma_{0}-term is polynomial in 1/ε1/\varepsilon. For the noise satisfying 𝔼​‖g⁡(x,ξ)−∇f​(x)‖α≲(f⁡(x)−f∗)ϱ\mathbb{E}\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|^{\alpha}\lesssim(f(x)-f^{*})^{\varrho}, the stochastic cost is polynomial, logarithmic, or bounded in 1/ε1/\varepsilon depending on whether ϱ\varrho is below, at, or above α\alpha for convex and α/2\alpha/2 for strongly convex objectives (their Theorem 11). Their lower bounds for the convex case and the σ0\sigma_{0}- and σ2\sigma_{2}-terms (their Theorems 13 and 15) are based on a two-point construction with a rare informative response, similar to the one used in our Propositions H.2 and H.3, and have the factor ln⁡(1/(2​ρ))\ln(1/(2\rho)) in terms of the failure probability ρ\rho.

The two works are complementary: Lobanov et al., (2026) consider generalized smoothness, strong convexity, and the noise decaying with the function gap, under moment bounds, and analyze a restarted and projected method whose parameters depend on the bound on f⁡(x0)−f∗f(x^{0})-f^{*}, DD, α\alpha, σi\sigma_{i}, and HiH_{i} (the horizon-driven variant from their Appendix I removes the last three from the inner updates, and their Appendix G constructs the initial bound from stochastic gradients); we consider Clip-SGD and Clip-SSTM without restarts and projections, under the tail condition on a ball, and also cover the weak-L2L^{2} endpoint with infinite variance, prescribed clipping levels, and the corresponding lower bounds.

Beyond moment bounds: symmetry, medians, and tail conditions.

Several approaches relax moment assumptions by imposing structure on the noise. Under symmetry, Jakovetić et al., (2023) analyze a general class of non-linear SGD methods (clipping, sign, normalization, and their component-wise versions) for strongly convex objectives under the noise whose components have a symmetric density and finite first moment only, and derive almost sure convergence and mean-squared-error rates; Armacki et al., (2023) derive high-probability bounds for non-convex and strongly convex problems in the same noise model, and Armacki et al., (2025) extend this framework to online learning, treating sign, quantization, and clipping non-linearities in a unified way, for symmetric noise without any moment assumption and for mixtures of symmetric and non-symmetric components, with convergence to a neighborhood in the latter case; Armacki et al., (2026) derive large-deviation and mean-squared-error bounds under a symmetric density that is positive near zero and possibly unbounded moments; Yu et al., (2026) obtain mean-squared-error rates for smoothed clipping with error feedback for decentralized strongly convex problems; and Kornilov et al., (2024) use median clipping for zeroth-order convex problems and bandits under symmetric noise with bounded κ\kappa-th moment for some κ>0\kappa>0, in which case the noise may have no finite expectation.

Puchkin et al., (2024) stabilize the stochastic gradients via smoothed medians of means before clipping and derive, under a structural condition on the marginal densities of the noise (a symmetric heavy-tailed part plus an antisymmetric remainder with finite second moment), high-probability rates for (quasi-)strongly convex problems of the order O~(K−1/2)\widetilde{O}(K^{-1/2}) in general, which improves upon the heavy-tailed rate O(K−2(α−1)/α)O(K^{-2(\alpha-1)/\alpha}) for α<4/3\alpha<4/3, and of the order O~​(K−1)\widetilde{O}(K^{-1}) for symmetric noise.

A tail condition also appears in Shestakov et al., (2026): there, a regularly varying tail ℙ{∥g(x∗,ξ)−∇f(x∗)∥≥u}∼cu−α\mathbb{P}\{\|g(x^{*},\xi)-\nabla f(x^{*})\|\geq u\}\sim cu^{-\alpha} at the minimizer quantifies how heavy-tailed data affect the finite-sum minimization and the generalization of ClipSGD, with the bounds in expectation over the algorithm.

The weak-LpL^{p} tail condition itself appears in El Bakkali et al., (2026), who impose it on the sample-gradient noise with a constant scale on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (their Assumption 1.3) for zeroth-order optimization of smooth non-convex objectives under global sample-wise LL-smoothness (their Assumption 1.2): their method clips the scalar directional derivatives of a two-point estimator before aggregation, and they derive high-probability guarantees for finding ε\varepsilon-stationary points using O~(dp/(2​(p−1))ε−(3p−2)/(p−1))\widetilde{O}(d^{p/(2(p-1))}\varepsilon^{-(3p-2)/(p-1)}) function evaluations, which gives O~​(d​ε−4)\widetilde{O}(d\varepsilon^{-4}) at p=2p=2 under a condition allowing infinite variance.

Their analysis of the base method controls the error of the estimator at every step separately, via a vector Bernstein inequality for the mini-batch and a union bound over the steps; therefore, their base method requires mini-batches of size Θ~​((d​(L⁡(f⁡(x0)−f∗)+σ)/ε)p/(p−1))\widetilde{\Theta}\big((\sqrt{d}\,(\sqrt{L(f(x^{0})-f^{*})}+\sigma)/\varepsilon)^{p/(p-1)}\big) at each of its O⁡(L⁡(f⁡(x0)−f∗)/ε2)O(L(f(x^{0})-f^{*})/\varepsilon^{2}) steps, where σ\sigma is their noise scale (their Remark 2.4); at p=2p=2, both the batch size and the number of steps grow as ε−2\varepsilon^{-2}.

Their momentum variant reduces the running batch size in proportion to one minus the momentum parameter, down to a single two-point estimate per step (two function evaluations with shared randomness), at the price of the stepsize reduced in the same proportion, a warm-start batch of the full size, and the same total number of function evaluations up to logarithmic factors and the additive warm-start cost (their Theorem 3.1 and Remark 3.2).

Our Assumption 3.5 differs from the symmetry-based and minimizer-based conditions in that it is a weak-LαL^{\alpha} bound on the whole ball QQ, without any symmetry or density assumptions; it has the same tail form as the condition from El Bakkali et al., (2026), in the affine and local version, and we use it for first-order methods on convex problems with one oracle call per iteration, where the polynomial rates coincide with those for the moment case. We characterize the additional logarithmic factor at the weak-L2L^{2} endpoint with infinite variance, analyze prescribed clipping levels, and derive lower bounds.

Methods without clipping can also converge under infinite variance (Wang et al.,, 2021; Fatkhullin et al.,, 2025; Liu, 2026b, ). These results and the in-expectation analysis under Hölder smoothness by Zaman and Mukherjee, (2026) use moment bounds. For convex composite problems, He et al., (2025) analyze an accelerated stochastic proximal method without clipping under a uniform bounded-moment assumption. Their heavy-tailed high-probability bounds have polynomial confidence dependence; logarithmic dependence is obtained under stronger sub-Weibull assumptions. Their bounded-domain and proximal setting differs from our local analysis of unconstrained first-order methods.

Non-convex problems and alternatives to clipping.

Zhang et al., 2020b () show that clipped SGD attains the optimal in-expectation rate K−(α−1)/(3α−2)K^{-(\alpha-1)/(3\alpha-2)} for the gradient norm under a bounded α\alpha-th moment assumption. Cutkosky and Mehta, (2021) derive high-probability bounds by combining clipping, normalization, and momentum. Liu et al., (2023) improve the analysis and obtain acceleration beyond the general lower bound when the objective is an expectation of smooth sample functions.

Hübler et al., (2025) analyze normalized SGD with mini-batches or momentum without clipping: they obtain in-expectation convergence without knowledge of the problem parameters and high-probability guarantees for the mini-batched variant. Liu and Zhou, (2025) show that normalized SGD with momentum and mini-batches achieves the optimal in-expectation rate when the tail index is known; when it is unknown, their rate is K−(α−1)/(2α)K^{-(\alpha-1)/(2\alpha)}. Sun et al., (2025) clarify the roles of normalization and clipping, and Kornilov et al., (2025) analyze sign methods with high probability under (L0,L1)(L_{0},L_{1})-smoothness. Li and Liu, (2022) obtain high-probability guarantees for non-convex SGD under sub-Weibull noise. These results concern non-convex objectives and complement our smooth convex analysis.

Affine and multiplicative noise.

Affine variance (Bottou et al.,, 2018), expected smoothness (Gower et al.,, 2019), and the ABC condition (Khaled and Richtárik,, 2023) are standard assumptions in the in-expectation analysis of SGD. Adaptive methods under affine variance are studied by Faw et al., (2022); Wang et al., (2023) and, under (L0,L1)(L_{0},L_{1})-smoothness, by Faw et al., (2023). These works concern non-convex objectives and include high-probability guarantees with polynomial dependence on the inverse failure probability. Attia and Koren, (2023) obtain high-probability bounds under an almost sure affine noise bound, with a sub-Gaussian extension; these assumptions exclude infinite variance.

State-dependent finite-variance bounds also appear in streaming estimation. For mean estimation and linear regression, Tsai et al., (2022) analyze clipped SGD with a decaying stepsize and variance growing quadratically with the distance to the solution. Their clipping level scales as N\sqrt{N} and depends on the confidence level, and their squared-error bound has order 1/N1/N with logarithmic confidence dependence. Das et al., (2024) derive high-probability guarantees for smooth strongly convex objectives under a covariance bound growing quadratically with the distance to the solution (their Assumption 2 and Theorem 2). Under infinite variance, Wang et al., (2021) analyze unmodified SGD with state-dependent noise and a finite pp-th moment, p∈[1,2)p\in[1,2), for a class of strongly convex objectives satisfying a pp-positive-definiteness condition on the Hessian. They obtain LpL^{p} rates and a generalized central limit theorem.

Multiplicative noise also explains how heavy-tailed iterates can arise from light-tailed data (Gürbüzbalaban et al.,, 2021; Hodgkinson and Mahoney,, 2021); Jiao and Keller-Ressel, (2024) study this phenomenon in homogenized SGD. Heavy-tailed gradient noise is documented and modeled by Şimşekli et al., (2019); Nguyen et al., (2019); Zhang et al., 2020b (), and Barsbey et al., (2021) relate heavy tails to compressibility and generalization. Under global strong growth or multiplicative finite-variance conditions, accelerated methods attain faster rates in expectation (Vaswani et al.,, 2019; Gupta et al.,, 2024); see the comparison in Appendix I.

Our assumptions combine a gradient-dependent scale with heavy tails. Replacing this scale by σ=σ0+σ1​supQ‖∇f‖\sigma=\sigma_{0}+\sigma_{1}\sup_{Q}\|\nabla f\| recovers a constant-scale condition but loses the separation between the additive and multiplicative contributions (Corollary I.9).

Prescribed clipping levels and clipping bias.

Clipping with a fixed level may introduce a persistent bias. Under bounded variance, Koloskova et al., (2023) derive tight in-expectation guarantees for convergence to a neighborhood and show that decreasing the stepsize alone cannot remove the bias. Chen et al., (2020) study this effect in private SGD through the symmetry of the gradient distribution. Mai and Johansson, (2021) establish stability estimates beyond Lipschitz continuity, including a fixed-threshold variant.

Zhang et al., 2020a () explain how clipping can accelerate optimization under (L0,L1)(L_{0},L_{1})-smoothness. For convex objectives in this class, Gorbunov et al., (2025) analyze gradient descent with smoothed clipping and its stochastic finite-sum variant under a common-minimizer assumption, in expectation. Gaash et al., (2025) derive high-probability bounds for clipped SGD with double sampling under sub-Gaussian noise, and El Bakkali El Kadi et al., (2025) obtain such bounds under a bounded α\alpha-th moment without exponentially large factors. Under strong growth and interpolation, Lobanov and Koloskova, (2026) analyze clipping and normalization under generalized smoothness and show that a suitable batch size can eliminate the error floor. Their heavy-tailed extension concerns normalized SGD and uses a moment bound.

Under standard smoothness and a bounded α\alpha-th moment, Khah et al., (2026) obtain high-probability guarantees for the best iterate with any clipping level. Our Theorem F.4 controls the averaged iterate under affine weak-LαL^{\alpha} noise for λ≥2​2​L​R\lambda\geq 2\sqrt{2}LR (and λ≥240​b​σ12​L​R\lambda\geq 240b\sigma_{1}^{2}LR when α=2\alpha=2 and σ1>0\sigma_{1}>0). Theorem G.1 covers any λ>0\lambda>0 for the best iterate when σ1≤σ¯1\sigma_{1}\leq\bar{\sigma}_{1} (under Assumption 3.5, for α<2\alpha<2). For additive noise, Theorem H.1 gives the unavoidable neighborhood 148⋅4α​min⁡{R​σ0α/λα−1,R​σ0,L​R2}\frac{1}{48\cdot 4^{\alpha}}\min\{R\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}/\lambda^{\alpha-1},R\sigma_{0},LR^{2}\} through a distribution satisfying the moment condition.

Lower bounds.

Stochastic convex lower bounds go back to Nemirovski and Yudin, (1983). Under infinite variance, Vural et al., (2022) prove that K−(α−1)/αK^{-(\alpha-1)/\alpha} is optimal for non-smooth convex problems and that Mirror Descent attains it in expectation. Zhang et al., 2020b () derive the non-convex counterpart K−(α−1)/(3α−2)K^{-(\alpha-1)/(3\alpha-2)}. Liu, 2026a () obtain high-probability and in-expectation lower bounds for non-smooth convex problems in terms of two noise scales.

Our Propositions H.2 and H.3 concern smooth unconstrained problems, give explicit constants, and capture the failure probability. Proposition I.16 establishes the necessity of the logarithmic factors on the Lorentz scale at α=2\alpha=2, in the regimes stated there. We do not derive a lower bound for the multiplicative-noise term.

Robust estimation.

Another approach replaces each stochastic gradient with a robust estimate computed from a batch, using, for example, coordinate-wise Catoni-type estimators (Holland and Ikeda,, 2019) or median-of-means-type estimators (Prasad et al.,, 2020). Lugosi and Mendelson, (2019) survey mean estimation under heavy tails. These analyses use batches to estimate the mean gradient, whereas the methods studied here clip individual stochastic gradients.

Appendix C Weak-LαL^{\alpha} and Marcinkiewicz Spaces

In this section, we recall the basic facts about weak-LαL^{\alpha} and Marcinkiewicz spaces that we use in the paper. Rearrangement-invariant function spaces are the natural language for power-law tails. Marcinkiewicz spaces are one of the basic classes of such spaces, along with Lorentz and Orlicz spaces; we refer to the monographs by Kreĭn et al., (1982), Bennett and Sharpley, (1988), Lindenstrauss and Tzafriri, (1979), and Braverman, (1994) for the details. The connection between rearrangement-invariant spaces and probabilistic inequalities for independent random variables is surveyed by Astashkin and Sukochev, (2010), and martingale inequalities in such spaces are studied by Kikuchi, (1999); Kikuchi, (2004). In this paper, we use the Marcinkiewicz space with fundamental function φ⁡(t)=t1/α\varphi(t)=t^{1/\alpha}; as a set, it coincides with weak-Lα=Lα,∞L^{\alpha}=L^{\alpha,\infty}.

Let YY be a real random variable on (Ω,ℱ,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}) with tail function dY(u):=ℙ{|Y|>u}d_{Y}(u):=\mathbb{P}\{|Y|>u\}, u≥0u\geq 0. Its non-increasing rearrangement Y∗:(0,1]→[0,∞]Y^{*}:(0,1]\to[0,\infty] and maximal rearrangement are defined as follows:

Y∗​(t)\displaystyle Y^{*}(t) :=inf{u>0:dY​(u)≤t},\displaystyle:=\inf\{u>0:\ d_{Y}(u)\leq t\},
Y∗⁣∗​(t)\displaystyle Y^{**}(t) :=1t​∫0tY∗​(s)​⁡𝑑s.\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{t}\int_{0}^{t}Y^{*}(s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s.
C.1Weak-LαL^{\alpha} quasi-norm.

For α>0\alpha>0, let

‖Y‖Lα,∞:=supu>0uℙ{|Y|>u}1/α=sup0<t≤1t1/αY∗(t),\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{L^{\alpha,\infty}}:=\sup_{u>0}u\,\mathbb{P}\{|Y|>u\}^{1/\alpha}=\sup_{0<t\leq 1}t^{1/\alpha}Y^{*}(t), (13)

and let Lα,∞L^{\alpha,\infty} be the set of all YY with ‖Y‖Lα,∞<∞\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{L^{\alpha,\infty}}<\infty.

The functional (13) is positively homogeneous and rearrangement invariant, but, in general, it does not satisfy the triangle inequality, i.e., it is only a quasi-norm (Bennett and Sharpley,, 1988). Nevertheless, for α>1\alpha>1, the same class of random variables admits an equivalent norm.

C.2Marcinkiewicz norm.

For α>1\alpha>1 and a random variable YY, let ‖Y‖Mα:=sup0<t≤1t1/α​Y∗⁣∗​(t)\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{M_{\alpha}}:=\sup_{0<t\leq 1}t^{1/\alpha}Y^{**}(t). The space MαM_{\alpha} of all YY with ‖Y‖Mα<∞\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{M_{\alpha}}<\infty is the Marcinkiewicz space with fundamental function φ⁡(t)=t1/α\varphi(t)=t^{1/\alpha}.

C.3Equivalence of weak-LαL^{\alpha} and MαM_{\alpha}.

For 1<α<∞1<\alpha<\infty, the spaces Lα,∞L^{\alpha,\infty} and MαM_{\alpha} coincide as sets and

‖Y‖Lα,∞≤‖Y‖Mα≤αα−1​‖Y‖Lα,∞.\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{L^{\alpha,\infty}}\leq\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{M_{\alpha}}\leq\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{L^{\alpha,\infty}}. (14)
C.4Fundamental function and monotonicity.

For every event A∈ℱA\in\mathcal{F}, ‖𝟏A‖Mα=ℙ​(A)1/α\left\lVert\mathbf{1}_{A}\right\rVert_{M_{\alpha}}=\mathbb{P}(A)^{1/\alpha}. If |Y|≤|Z||Y|\leq|Z| almost surely, then ‖Y‖Mα≤‖Z‖Mα\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{M_{\alpha}}\leq\left\lVert Z\right\rVert_{M_{\alpha}}. The norm depends only on the distribution of |Y||Y|, i.e., MαM_{\alpha} is rearrangement invariant.

Therefore, the absence of the triangle inequality for the tail quasi-norm does not cause any difficulties in the clipping lemma (Lemma D.1): it is convenient to prove the lemma using the quasi-norm, and one can always pass to the equivalent Marcinkiewicz norm. The next statement clarifies the exact relation between the moment and the weak-LαL^{\alpha} settings.

C.5Embeddings.

Let α>0\alpha>0.

  1. 1.

    If Y∈LαY\in L^{\alpha}, then ‖Y‖Lα,∞≤(𝔼​|Y|α)1/α\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{L^{\alpha,\infty}}\leq\left(\mathbb{E}|Y|^{\alpha}\right)^{1/\alpha}.

  2. 2.

    If Y∈Lα,∞Y\in L^{\alpha,\infty} and 0<q<α0<q<\alpha, then Y∈LqY\in L^{q} and

    𝔼​|Y|q≤αα−q​‖Y‖Lα,∞q.\mathbb{E}|Y|^{q}\leq\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-q}\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{L^{\alpha,\infty}}^{q}. (15)

In general, Y∈Lα,∞Y\in L^{\alpha,\infty} does not imply Y∈LαY\in L^{\alpha}.

C.6Direction of the implications.

For the same exponent α\alpha, weak-LαL^{\alpha} control does not imply a bound on the α\alpha-th moment. The correct statements are the following: strong LαL^{\alpha} control implies weak-LαL^{\alpha} control with the same constant, and weak-LαL^{\alpha} control implies finiteness of every moment of order q<αq<\alpha with the explicit constant (15). In particular, Assumption 3.5 implies Assumption 3.4 with α\alpha replaced by any q∈(1,α)q\in(1,\alpha) and σj\sigma_{j} replaced by (α/(α−q))1/q​σj(\alpha/(\alpha-q))^{1/q}\sigma_{j}, j∈{0,1}j\in\{0,1\} (it is sufficient to use (15) and (s+t)q/α≤sq/α+tq/α(s+t)^{q/\alpha}\leq s^{q/\alpha}+t^{q/\alpha}). That is, it is the result obtained under the weaker assumption that is stronger.

The following example, which we summarize in Section 3, shows that the strict inclusion Lα⊊Lα,∞L^{\alpha}\subsetneq L^{\alpha,\infty} is attained by the simplest heavy-tailed oracle. λα:=(2​αα−1)1/(α−1),p:=λα−α,d:=12​(1−p).{\lambda_{\alpha}:=\left(\frac{2\alpha}{\alpha-1}\right)^{1/(\alpha-1)},\qquad p:=\lambda_{\alpha}^{-\alpha},\qquad d:=\frac{1}{2(1-p)}.}

Let Y≥λαY\geq\lambda_{\alpha} have the Pareto tail ℙ{Y>u}=(λα/u)α\mathbb{P}\{Y>u\}=(\lambda_{\alpha}/u)^{\alpha} for u≥λαu\geq\lambda_{\alpha}, and let XX equal an independent copy of YY with probability pp and equal −d-d otherwise. Since p​𝔼​Y=p​α​λα/(α−1)=1/2=(1−p)​dp\mathbb{E}Y=p\alpha\lambda_{\alpha}/(\alpha-1)=1/2=(1-p)d, we have 𝔼​X=0\mathbb{E}X=0. Also, λα≥4\lambda_{\alpha}\geq 4, p≤1/4p\leq 1/4, and d<1d<1. For u<du<d the tail bound ℙ{|X|>u}≤u−α\mathbb{P}\{|X|>u\}\leq u^{-\alpha} is trivial; for d≤u<λαd\leq u<\lambda_{\alpha} it follows from p≤u−αp\leq u^{-\alpha}; and for u≥λαu\geq\lambda_{\alpha} it is an equality. Therefore, ‖X‖Lα,∞=1\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{L^{\alpha,\infty}}=1, while

|𝔼​clip​(X,λα)|=12−p​λα=12​α=λα1−αα−1.{\big|\mathbb{E}\texttt{clip}(X,\lambda_{\alpha})\big|=\frac{1}{2}-p\lambda_{\alpha}=\frac{1}{2\alpha}=\frac{\lambda_{\alpha}^{1-\alpha}}{\alpha-1}.}

Consequently, any bias constant valid uniformly over centered weak-LαL^{\alpha} noise is at least 1/(α−1)1/(\alpha-1). D.5Conditional versions.

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a σ\sigma-algebra, let xx be 𝒢\mathcal{G}-measurable, and let 𝔼⁡[X∣𝒢]=x\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]=x and ‖x‖≤λ/2\|x\|\leq\lambda/2. If, almost surely, ℙ⁡{‖X−x‖>u∣𝒢}≤A⁡(x)​u−α\mathbb{P}\{\|X-x\|>u\mid\mathcal{G}\}\leq A(x)u^{-\alpha} for all u>0u>0 (resp. 𝔼⁡[‖X−x‖α∣𝒢]≤A⁡(x)\mathbb{E}[\|X-x\|^{\alpha}\mid\mathcal{G}]\leq A(x)), then the conclusions of Lemma D.1 (resp. Lemma D.2) hold almost surely with 𝔼⁡[⋅]\mathbb{E}[\cdot] replaced by 𝔼[⋅∣𝒢]\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid\mathcal{G}]; in particular, ‖X~−𝔼⁡[X~∣𝒢]‖≤2​λ\|\widetilde{X}-\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{X}\mid\mathcal{G}]\|\leq 2\lambda almost surely.

Proof.

All steps of the proofs of Lemmas D.1 and D.2 remain valid after replacing expectations and probabilities with their conditional counterparts given 𝒢\mathcal{G}. The quantity A⁡(x)A(x) is 𝒢\mathcal{G}-measurable and, therefore, plays the role of a fixed coefficient in the conditional integral bounds. The conditional tail bounds can be assumed to hold for all u>0u>0 simultaneously on one event of full probability: it is sufficient to take versions for rational uu and extend them by monotonicity and right-continuity. Then, the conditional Tonelli theorem gives, for deterministic c>0c>0, 𝔼⁡[(Y−c)+∣𝒢]=∫c∞ℙ⁡{Y>u∣𝒢}​⁡𝑑u\mathbb{E}[(Y-c)_{+}\mid\mathcal{G}]=\int_{c}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}\{Y>u\mid\mathcal{G}\}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u and 𝔼⁡[min⁡{Y2,c2}∣𝒢]=2​∫0cu​ℙ​{Y>u∣𝒢}​⁡𝑑u\mathbb{E}[\min\{Y^{2},c^{2}\}\mid\mathcal{G}]=2\int_{0}^{c}u\,\mathbb{P}\{Y>u\mid\mathcal{G}\}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u, which we use with c=λ/2c=\lambda/2 and c=3​λ/2c=3\lambda/2. For Lemma D.2, the two pointwise inequalities from its proof have deterministic coefficients and remain valid after taking conditional expectations, with A⁡(x)A(x) replaced by any finite 𝒢\mathcal{G}-measurable upper bound on 𝔼⁡[‖X−x‖α∣𝒢]\mathbb{E}[\|X-x\|^{\alpha}\mid\mathcal{G}]. Finally, the conditional variance decomposition reads 𝔼⁡[‖X~−x‖2∣𝒢]=𝔼⁡[‖X~−𝔼⁡[X~∣𝒢]‖2∣𝒢]+‖𝔼⁡[X~∣𝒢]−x‖2\mathbb{E}[\|\widetilde{X}-x\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{G}]=\mathbb{E}[\|\widetilde{X}-\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{X}\mid\mathcal{G}]\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{G}]+\|\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{X}\mid\mathcal{G}]-x\|^{2}, which concludes the proof. ∎

Proof.

For s>0s>0, we have ϕ⁡(s)=(32)2−α​min⁡{2​s2−α,s+2α​h​(s)}\phi(s)=(\frac{3}{2})^{2-\alpha}\min\{\frac{2s}{2-\alpha},\,s+\frac{2}{\alpha}h(s)\} with h⁡(s):=s​ln⁡(1+C/s)h(s):=s\ln(1+C/s), where the first term is absent for α=2\alpha=2. Moreover, 0≤h⁡(s)=s​ln⁡(s+C)−s​ln⁡s→00\leq h(s)=s\ln(s+C)-s\ln s\to 0 as s↓0s\downarrow 0. Thus, with h⁡(0):=0h(0):=0, the function hh is continuous, concave, and non-decreasing on [0,∞)[0,\infty). Appendix E Auxiliary Results

Measurability conventions.

In the setting of Section 3, the oracle g⁡(x,ξ)g(x,\xi) is a jointly measurable and finite vector field with 𝔼ξ​[g⁡(x,ξ)]=∇f​(x)\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[g(x,\xi)]=\nabla f(x) for x∈Qx\in Q; we do not assume any sample-wise gradient representation. The noise g​(x,ξ)−∇f​(x)g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x) is controlled only at the points x∈Qx\in Q; Lemma I.3 (see Appendix I.2) transfers these pointwise conditions to random query points in QQ. Outside QQ, gg is an arbitrary jointly measurable and finite extension, ff is not necessarily differentiable, and, for definiteness, we set ∇f​(x):=0\nabla f(x):=0 there; this extension is used only to define auxiliary random variables on the whole probability space, and it never enters the bounds, which are derived on the events where the relevant points belong to QQ.

We assume that f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is Borel measurable; no differentiability, smoothness, or convexity is required outside QQ. Consequently, the objective gaps used in the auxiliary random variables and stopping times are measurable on the whole probability space.

The gradient bound.

Assumption 3.2 is stated separately to simplify the comparison with Sadiev et al., (2023); however, it is implied by the other two local assumptions, since QQ is a ball centered at the minimizer.

E.1Gradient bound from local smoothness and convexity.

Let ff be differentiable on Q=Br​(x∗)Q=B_{r}(x^{*}), r>0r>0, where x∗x^{*} is a minimizer of ff on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and let Assumptions 3.1 and 3.3 hold on QQ. Then ‖∇f​(x)‖2≤2​L​(f⁡(x)−f∗)\|\nabla f(x)\|^{2}\leq 2L(f(x)-f^{*}) for all x∈Qx\in Q.

Proof.

Step 1: cocoercivity on QQ. We claim that ⟨∇f​(x)−∇f​(z),x−z⟩≥1L​‖∇f​(x)−∇f​(z)‖2\left\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(z),x-z\right\rangle\geq\frac{1}{L}\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(z)\|^{2} for all x,z∈Qx,z\in Q. (a) First, we assume that ff is twice continuously differentiable on an open convex set UU on which Assumptions 3.1 and 3.3 hold, and let x,z∈Ux,z\in U. Then ∇f​(x)−∇f​(z)=A⁡(x−z)\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(z)=A(x-z) with A:=∫01∇2f​(z+t⁡(x−z))​⁡𝑑tA:=\int_{0}^{1}\nabla^{2}f(z+t(x-z))\,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t. Convexity gives ∇2f⪰0\nabla^{2}f\succeq 0 on UU and the Lipschitz bound gives ∇2f⪯L​I\nabla^{2}f\preceq LI on UU; hence, 0⪯A⪯L​I0\preceq A\preceq LI. Since AA and L​I−ALI-A commute, we have A⁡(L​I−A)⪰0A(LI-A)\succeq 0, i.e., A2⪯L​AA^{2}\preceq LA, and, therefore, ‖A⁡(x−z)‖2≤L⁡⟨A⁡(x−z),x−z⟩\|A(x-z)\|^{2}\leq L\left\langle A(x-z),x-z\right\rangle, which is exactly the claim. (b) In the general case, let ρδ\rho_{\delta} be a smooth probability density supported in Bδ​(0)B_{\delta}(0) and fδ:=f∗ρδf_{\delta}:=f*\rho_{\delta} on Uδ:={x:‖x−x∗‖<r−δ}U_{\delta}:=\{x:\|x-x^{*}\|<r-\delta\}. For x∈Uδx\in U_{\delta} and ‖u‖≤δ\|u\|\leq\delta, we have x−u∈Qx-u\in Q, meaning that fδf_{\delta} is well-defined and smooth on UδU_{\delta}, convex on UδU_{\delta} as an average of the convex functions x↦f⁡(x−u)x\mapsto f(x-u), and ∇fδ=(∇f)∗ρδ\nabla f_{\delta}=(\nabla f)*\rho_{\delta} is LL-Lipschitz on UδU_{\delta}; moreover, ‖∇fδ​(x)−∇f​(x)‖≤L​δ\|\nabla f_{\delta}(x)-\nabla f(x)\|\leq L\delta for x∈Uδx\in U_{\delta}. Applying (a) to fδf_{\delta} on UδU_{\delta} and letting δ→0\delta\to 0, we get the claim for all x,zx,z from the open ball {∥x−x∗∥<r}\{\|x-x^{*}\|<r\}, and then for all x,z∈Qx,z\in Q by the continuity of ∇f\nabla f on QQ.

Step 2. Let x∈Qx\in Q. Since x∗x^{*} is an interior point of QQ minimizing ff on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, we have ∇f​(x∗)=0\nabla f(x^{*})=0, and Step 1 with z=x∗z=x^{*} gives ⟨∇f​(x),x−x∗⟩≥1L​‖∇f​(x)‖2\left\langle\nabla f(x),x-x^{*}\right\rangle\geq\frac{1}{L}\|\nabla f(x)\|^{2}. Next, let y:=x−1L∇f(x)y:=x-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f(x). Then

‖y−x∗‖2=‖x−x∗‖2−2L​⟨∇f​(x),x−x∗⟩+1L2​‖∇f​(x)‖2≤‖x−x∗‖2−1L2​‖∇f​(x)‖2≤r2,\|y-x^{*}\|^{2}=\|x-x^{*}\|^{2}-\frac{2}{L}\left\langle\nabla f(x),x-x^{*}\right\rangle+\frac{1}{L^{2}}\|\nabla f(x)\|^{2}\leq\|x-x^{*}\|^{2}-\frac{1}{L^{2}}\|\nabla f(x)\|^{2}\leq r^{2},

Throughout the appendix, we use the following decomposition of the error of the clipped stochastic gradient (with the convention ∇f:=0\nabla f:=0 outside QQ, meaning that all quantities below are defined on the whole probability space):

θk:=g~k−∇f​(xk)=θku+θkb,θku:=g~k−𝔼⁡[g~k∣𝒢k],θkb:=𝔼⁡[g~k∣𝒢k]−∇f​(xk),\theta_{k}:=\widetilde{g}^{k}-\nabla f(x^{k})=\theta_{k}^{u}+\theta_{k}^{b},\qquad\theta_{k}^{u}:=\widetilde{g}^{k}-\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{g}^{k}\mid\mathcal{G}_{k}],\qquad\theta_{k}^{b}:=\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{g}^{k}\mid\mathcal{G}_{k}]-\nabla f(x^{k}), (25)

where 𝔼⁡[θku∣𝒢k]=0\mathbb{E}[\theta_{k}^{u}\mid\mathcal{G}_{k}]=0 by construction.

E.2Basic inequality.

Let Assumptions 3.2 and 3.3 hold on QQ, let 0<γ≤1/(2​L)0<\gamma\leq 1/(2L), and let x0,…,xt−1∈Qx^{0},\dots,x^{t-1}\in Q for some integer t≥1t\geq 1. Then

γ​∑l=0t−1(f⁡(xl)−f∗)\displaystyle\gamma\sum_{l=0}^{t-1}\left(f(x^{l})-f^{*}\right) ≤∥x0−x∗∥2−∥xt−x∗∥2−2γ∑l=0t−1⟨xl−x∗−γ∇f(xl),θl⟩+γ2∑l=0t−1∥θl∥2,\displaystyle\leq\|x^{0}-x^{*}\|^{2}-\|x^{t}-x^{*}\|^{2}-2\gamma\sum_{l=0}^{t-1}\left\langle x^{l}-x^{*}-\gamma\nabla f(x^{l}),\theta_{l}\right\rangle+\gamma^{2}\sum_{l=0}^{t-1}\|\theta_{l}\|^{2}, (26)

and the left-hand side of (26) is at least γ​t​(f⁡(x¯t−1)−f∗)\gamma t\left(f(\bar{x}^{t-1})-f^{*}\right), where x¯t−1:=1t​∑l=0t−1xl\bar{x}^{t-1}:=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{l=0}^{t-1}x^{l}.

Proof.

By the update rule, we have xl+1=xl−γ∇f(xl)−γθlx^{l+1}=x^{l}-\gamma\nabla f(x^{l})-\gamma\theta_{l}. Expanding the squared distance to x∗x^{*}, we get

‖xl+1−x∗‖2\displaystyle\|x^{l+1}-x^{*}\|^{2} =‖xl−x∗‖2−2​γ​⟨xl−x∗,∇f​(xl)⟩+γ2​‖∇f​(xl)‖2\displaystyle=\|x^{l}-x^{*}\|^{2}-2\gamma\left\langle x^{l}-x^{*},\nabla f(x^{l})\right\rangle+\gamma^{2}\|\nabla f(x^{l})\|^{2}
−2γ⟨xl−x∗−γ∇f(xl),θl⟩+γ2∥θl∥2.\displaystyle\quad-2\gamma\left\langle x^{l}-x^{*}-\gamma\nabla f(x^{l}),\theta_{l}\right\rangle+\gamma^{2}\|\theta_{l}\|^{2}.

By convexity, we have ⟨xl−x∗,∇f​(xl)⟩≥f⁡(xl)−f∗\left\langle x^{l}-x^{*},\nabla f(x^{l})\right\rangle\geq f(x^{l})-f^{*}. By Assumption 3.2 and γ≤1/(2​L)\gamma\leq 1/(2L), we also have γ2​‖∇f​(xl)‖2≤2​L​γ2​(f⁡(xl)−f∗)≤γ⁡(f⁡(xl)−f∗)\gamma^{2}\|\nabla f(x^{l})\|^{2}\leq 2L\gamma^{2}(f(x^{l})-f^{*})\leq\gamma(f(x^{l})-f^{*}). Therefore,

γ(f(xl)−f∗)≤∥xl−x∗∥2−∥xl+1−x∗∥2−2γ⟨xl−x∗−γ∇f(xl),θl⟩+γ2∥θl∥2.\gamma\left(f(x^{l})-f^{*}\right)\leq\|x^{l}-x^{*}\|^{2}-\|x^{l+1}-x^{*}\|^{2}-2\gamma\left\langle x^{l}-x^{*}-\gamma\nabla f(x^{l}),\theta_{l}\right\rangle+\gamma^{2}\|\theta_{l}\|^{2}.

Summing up the above inequality over l=0,…,t−1l=0,\dots,t-1, we get (26). The last claim follows from Jensen’s inequality for the convex function ff on the convex set Q∋x¯t−1Q\ni\bar{x}^{t-1}, which concludes the proof. ∎

E.3Freedman’s inequality.

Let (ℱi)i≥0(\mathcal{F}_{i})_{i\geq 0} be a filtration and let XiX_{i} be ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i}-measurable with 𝔼⁡[Xi∣ℱi−1]=0\mathbb{E}[X_{i}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]=0 and |Xi|≤c|X_{i}|\leq c almost surely. Let vi:=𝔼⁡[Xi2∣ℱi−1]v_{i}:=\mathbb{E}[X_{i}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]. Then for all b,G>0b,G>0,

ℙ{|∑i=1nXi|>b and ∑i=1nvi≤G}≤2exp(−b22​G+2​c​b/3).\mathbb{P}\left\{\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\right|>b\ \text{ and }\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}\leq G\right\}\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{b^{2}}{2G+2cb/3}\right). (27)

The same bound holds for the larger event {∃m≤n:|∑i=1mXi|>b​ and ​∑i=1mvi≤G}\big\{\exists m\leq n:\ |\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_{i}|>b\ \text{ and }\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}v_{i}\leq G\big\} (maximal form).

Proof.

This is the martingale version of Bernstein’s inequality (Freedman,, 1975; Dzhaparidze and Van Zanten,, 2001); for completeness, we provide the full proof. For c=0c=0, the claim is trivial; therefore, we assume that c>0c>0. Since m!≥2⋅3m−2m!\geq 2\cdot 3^{m-2} for m≥2m\geq 2, for |x|≤c|x|\leq c and 0<μ<3/c0<\mu<3/c we have

eμ​x≤1+μ​x+μ2​x22​∑j=0∞(μ​c3)j=1+μ​x+μ2​x22​(1−μ​c/3).e^{\mu x}\leq 1+\mu x+\frac{\mu^{2}x^{2}}{2}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\mu c}{3}\right)^{j}=1+\mu x+\frac{\mu^{2}x^{2}}{2(1-\mu c/3)}.

Let ψ⁡(μ):=μ22​(1−μ​c/3)\psi(\mu):=\frac{\mu^{2}}{2(1-\mu c/3)}. Taking conditional expectations and using 1+u≤eu1+u\leq e^{u}, we get 𝔼⁡[eμ​Xi∣ℱi−1]≤exp⁡(ψ⁡(μ)​vi)\mathbb{E}[e^{\mu X_{i}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]\leq\exp(\psi(\mu)v_{i}). Thus, Mm:=exp⁡(μ​∑i≤mXi−ψ⁡(μ)​∑i≤mvi)M_{m}:=\exp\left(\mu\sum_{i\leq m}X_{i}-\psi(\mu)\sum_{i\leq m}v_{i}\right) is a non-negative supermartingale with M0=1M_{0}=1, implying 𝔼​Mn≤1\mathbb{E}M_{n}\leq 1. On the event {∑i≤nXi>b,∑i≤nvi≤G}\{\sum_{i\leq n}X_{i}>b,\ \sum_{i\leq n}v_{i}\leq G\}, we have Mn>eμ​b−ψ⁡(μ)​GM_{n}>e^{\mu b-\psi(\mu)G}; by Markov’s inequality, the probability of this event is at most e−μ​b+ψ⁡(μ)​Ge^{-\mu b+\psi(\mu)G}. The choice μ=bG+c​b/3<3c\mu=\frac{b}{G+cb/3}<\frac{3}{c} gives −μ​b+ψ⁡(μ)​G=−b22​G+2​c​b/3-\mu b+\psi(\mu)G=-\frac{b^{2}}{2G+2cb/3}. Applying the same bound to −Xi-X_{i} and taking the union of the two events, we get (27). To prove the maximal form, note that on {∃m≤n:∑i≤mXi>b,∑i≤mvi≤G}\{\exists m\leq n:\sum_{i\leq m}X_{i}>b,\ \sum_{i\leq m}v_{i}\leq G\} we have maxm≤n⁡Mm>eμ​b−ψ⁡(μ)​G\max_{m\leq n}M_{m}>e^{\mu b-\psi(\mu)G}, and Ville’s maximal inequality for the non-negative supermartingale (Mm)(M_{m}), ℙ{maxm≤nMm≥a}≤𝔼M0/a\mathbb{P}\{\max_{m\leq n}M_{m}\geq a\}\leq\mathbb{E}M_{0}/a, gives the same bound e−μ​b+ψ⁡(μ)​Ge^{-\mu b+\psi(\mu)G} (Freedman,, 1975, Theorem 1.6), which concludes the proof. ∎

E.4Jensen for powers.

For 0<r≤10<r\leq 1 and non-negative a1,…,ana_{1},\dots,a_{n}, ∑i=1nair≤n1−r​(∑i=1nai)r\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}^{r}\leq n^{1-r}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\right)^{r}.

Proof.

The function t↦trt\mapsto t^{r} is concave for 0<r≤10<r\leq 1, and, by Jensen’s inequality, 1n​∑i=1nair≤(1n​∑i=1nai)r\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}^{r}\leq\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\right)^{r}. Multiplying both sides by nn, we get the claim. ∎

Discussion.

If we write λ0=ρ​σ0\lambda_{0}=\rho\sigma_{0} in (36), then the price of misspecifying the noise level is the factor 80​ρ​ℓ+120​b​ρ1−α+120​2​v​ℓ​ρ1−α/280\rho\ell+120b\rho^{1-\alpha}+120\sqrt{2v\ell}\,\rho^{1-\alpha/2} in front of σ0R(K+1)−(α−1)/α\sigma_{0}R(K+1)^{-(\alpha-1)/\alpha}, which grows linearly in the case of overestimation (ρ→∞\rho\to\infty) and as ρ−(α−1)\rho^{-(\alpha-1)} in the case of underestimation (ρ→0\rho\to 0). We emphasize that Theorems F.1 and F.4 both follow from one general bound (Proposition F.6 below), where γ\gamma and λ\lambda are coupled only through the bias condition, involving bb, and the variance condition, involving vv; under Assumption 3.4, Theorem F.1 is the special case λ=R/(40​γ​ℓ)\lambda=R/(40\gamma\ell) of Theorem F.4, while under Assumption 3.5 the variance constants vα​(ΛK)v_{\alpha}(\Lambda_{K}) and vα​(Λλ)v_{\alpha}(\Lambda_{\lambda}) are not comparable in general, meaning that neither of the theorems contains the other one. For σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0 and the moment condition, the bound of Khah et al., (2026), for λ>4​L​R\lambda>4LR and the best iterate, reduces to the same three terms as in Corollary F.5 after applying the initial-point bound f⁡(x0)−f∗≤L​R2/2f(x^{0})-f^{*}\leq LR^{2}/2 (see the discussion of Table 3): a λ​R​ℓ/K\lambda R\ell/K term, a neighborhood of the order R​σ0α/λα−1R\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}/\lambda^{\alpha-1}, and a cross term of the order R​λ1−α/2​σ0α/2​ℓ/KR\lambda^{1-\alpha/2}\sigma_{0}^{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\ell/K}; Corollary F.5 gives them for the averaged iterate, under affine weak-LαL^{\alpha} noise and with explicit constants, and, at α=2\alpha=2 under Assumption 3.5, only the cross term has the logarithm of v2v_{2}.

and let c:=180​max⁡{v,b/3}c:=180\max\{v,b/3\}, meaning that

F.6A general high-probability bound.

Let Assumptions 3.1–3.3 hold for Q=B2​R​(x∗)Q=B_{2R}(x^{*}), where R≥‖x0−x∗‖>0R\geq\|x^{0}-x^{*}\|>0, and let either Assumption 3.4 or Assumption 3.5 hold with α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2]. Let β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), K∈{0,1,…}K\in\{0,1,\dots\}, and let γ,λ>0\gamma,\lambda>0 satisfy, with (b,v)(b,v) defined above,

Then, with probability at least 1−β1-\beta, the iterates produced by Algorithm 1 with λk≡λ\lambda_{k}\equiv\lambda satisfy xk∈B2​R​(x∗)x^{k}\in B_{\sqrt{2}R}(x^{*}) for all k=0,1,…,K+1k=0,1,\dots,K+1 and f⁡(x¯K)−f∗≤2​R2γ⁡(K+1)f(\bar{x}^{K})-f^{*}\leq\frac{2R^{2}}{\gamma(K+1)}.

The third condition in (40) controls the accumulated clipping bias, and the fourth one controls the accumulated variance. Both of them follow from the single condition ΦK+1≤3​R/c\Phi_{K+1}\leq 3R/c: by (39), b​ΦK+1≤3​b​R/c≤R/20b\Phi_{K+1}\leq 3bR/c\leq R/20, and v​γ2​λ2−α​ΣK+1=v​γ​λ​ΦK+1≤R40​ℓ⋅3​v​Rc≤R22400​ℓv\gamma^{2}\lambda^{2-\alpha}\Sigma_{K+1}=v\,\gamma\lambda\,\Phi_{K+1}\leq\frac{R}{40\ell}\cdot\frac{3vR}{c}\leq\frac{R^{2}}{2400\ell}. This is exactly how we derive Theorem F.1 below. For a prescribed λ\lambda, keeping the two conditions separate is what makes the neighborhood in Theorem F.4 independent of the variance constant vv (and of its logarithm at α=2\alpha=2).

Proof of Proposition F.6.

Our proof is induction-based: by induction, we show that the iterates do not leave the ball B2​R​(x∗)B_{\sqrt{2}R}(x^{*}) with high probability. We start with the consequences of (40). By the first two conditions and ℓ>1\ell>1, we have

γ≤R40​ℓ​λ≤180​2​L<12​L,L​γ≤2−1,γ​λ≤R40​ℓ≤R40,2​L​R≤λ2.\gamma\leq\frac{R}{40\ell\lambda}\leq\frac{1}{80\sqrt{2}L}<\frac{1}{2L},\qquad L\gamma\leq\sqrt{2}-1,\qquad\gamma\lambda\leq\frac{R}{40\ell}\leq\frac{R}{40},\qquad\sqrt{2}LR\leq\frac{\lambda}{2}. (41)

To formulate the statement rigorously, we introduce probability event EkE_{k} for each k=0,1,…,K+1k=0,1,\dots,K+1 as follows: E0:=ΩE_{0}:=\Omega and, for k=1,…,K+1k=1,\dots,K+1,
