(42)

We will prove by induction that ℙ⁡(Ek)≥1−k​βK+1\mathbb{P}(E_{k})\geq 1-\frac{k\beta}{K+1} for all k=0,1,…,K+1k=0,1,\dots,K+1. The base of the induction (k=0k=0) is trivial. Next, we assume that the statement holds for k=T−1k=T-1 with some T∈{1,…,K+1}T\in\{1,\dots,K+1\}, i.e., ℙ⁡(ET−1)≥1−(T−1)​βK+1\mathbb{P}(E_{T-1})\geq 1-\frac{(T-1)\beta}{K+1}. Given this, we need to prove that ℙ⁡(ET)≥1−T​βK+1\mathbb{P}(E_{T})\geq 1-\frac{T\beta}{K+1}. Throughout the proof, empty sums are equal to zero.

First, we show that ET−1E_{T-1} implies that the iterates x0,…,xTx^{0},\dots,x^{T} belong to QQ. Upper bound for ③.

Let Yt:=2​γ2​(‖θtu‖2−𝔼⁡[‖θtu‖2∣𝒢t])Y_{t}:=2\gamma^{2}\left(\|\theta_{t}^{u}\|^{2}-\mathbb{E}[\|\theta_{t}^{u}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{G}_{t}]\right). Then {Yt}t=0T−1\{Y_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T-1} is a martingale difference sequence w.r.t. {𝒢t+1}t=0T−1\{\mathcal{G}_{t+1}\}_{t=0}^{T-1}, and, since ‖θtu‖2≤4​λ2\|\theta_{t}^{u}\|^{2}\leq 4\lambda^{2}, the summands are bounded:

Next, for a random variable 0≤Z≤B0\leq Z\leq B, we have 𝔼​(Z−𝔼​Z)2≤𝔼​Z2≤B​𝔼​Z\mathbb{E}(Z-\mathbb{E}Z)^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}Z^{2}\leq B\,\mathbb{E}Z. That is, we derived the upper bounds for ①–⑤. More precisely, ET−1∩E①∩E③E_{T-1}\cap E_{\text{①}}\cap E_{\text{③}} implies that all five bounds hold. Appendix H Lower Bounds for a Fixed Clipping Level: Full Statement, Comparison and Proofs

H.1 Full Statement and Comparison with Existing Results

In Table 3, we compare Theorems 5.3, 5.4, and 5.5 with Koloskova et al., (2023) and Khah et al., (2026); see also the comparison in Section 5.3. The table separates the output criterion, the neighborhood, and the terms that vanish with the horizon. We then give the full statement of Theorem 5.5, including the growth of the expected error with the total stepsize.

Here R≥‖x0−x∗‖R\geq\|x^{0}-x^{*}\|, xtx^{t} are the iterates with λk≡λ\lambda_{k}\equiv\lambda, and x¯K\bar{x}^{K} is their average. The noise is additive (σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0), with level σ0\sigma_{0} and index α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2], under Assumption 3.4 or 3.5. Unless a note states otherwise, the upper bounds hold with probability at least 1−β1-\beta, with a stepsize chosen for the horizon KK. The criterion is bounded by the neighborhood plus the vanishing terms. The vanishing terms suppress constants depending on α\alpha and logarithmic factors in KK and 1/β1/\beta.

Our neighborhood terms retain their constants: b=bαmom∈[1/2,1]b=b_{\alpha}^{\rm mom}\in[1/2,1] under Assumption 3.4, and b=bα=2α−1/(α−1)b=b_{\alpha}=2^{\alpha-1}/(\alpha-1) under Assumption 3.5. Theorems 3.1–3.2 of Koloskova et al., (2023) construct, for every λ>0\lambda>0, a one-dimensional strongly convex quadratic with L=1L=1 and two-point noise of variance σ02\sigma_{0}^{2}, for which every fixed point x^\hat{x} of the mean clipped field, 𝔼​clip​(g⁡(x^,ξ),λ)=0\mathbb{E}\texttt{clip}(g(\hat{x},\xi),\lambda)=0, satisfies the displayed gradient bound. Theorem H.1 gives the expected lower bound for every iterate and every convex combination with deterministic weights, under any positive deterministic stepsize sequence. H.3 Optimality of the Stochastic Term

H.2Lower bound for the stochastic term.

Let L,R,σ0>0L,R,\sigma_{0}>0, α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2], K∈{0,1,…}K\in\{0,1,\dots\}, and

Proposition H.2 establishes the optimal polynomial dependence of the additive stochastic term Δ0\Delta_{0} from Corollary F.2 on KK, σ0\sigma_{0}, and RR in the regime σ0R(K+1)−(α−1)/α≲LR2\sigma_{0}R(K+1)^{-(\alpha-1)/\alpha}\lesssim LR^{2}, at a fixed confidence level with failure probability below 1/41/4, within the class of algorithms using K+1K+1 oracle calls; Clip-SGD with K+1K+1 iterations belongs to this class. For the moment class, the upper and lower bounds match up to constants and the factor ℓ(α−1)/α\ell^{(\alpha-1)/\alpha}; at the weak-L2L^{2} endpoint, the upper bound also contains the tail-dependent logarithmic factor c2​(ΛK)1/2c_{2}(\Lambda_{K})^{1/2}. It is worth mentioning that the proposition itself does not establish the necessity of these logarithms, the optimal dependence on the failure probability, or the optimality of the multiplicative term; the dependence on the failure probability is studied in Proposition H.3 below, the necessity of the logarithm at α=2\alpha=2 at fixed confidence is shown in Proposition I.16, and nothing is claimed for the multiplicative term. The hard instances have bounded gradients, |fv′|≤s|f_{v}^{\prime}|\leq s, and state-dependent noise (its law depends on xx through δ⁡(x)\delta(x), which is allowed by Assumption 3.4); therefore, the lower bound also holds within the subclass of problems with bounded gradients. That is, the proposition concerns a uniformly bounded noise scale (σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0) rather than state-independent additive noise; in contrast, the Lorentz lower bound from Proposition I.16 (see Appendix I.8) is realized by state-independent noise. Related lower bounds are classical in expectation (Nemirovski and Yudin,, 1983; Vural et al.,, 2022), and Liu, 2026a () recently proves high-probability lower bounds for non-smooth convex problems under bounded α\alpha-th moments, of the order (σs2/α−1​σl2−2/α+σs​ln1−1/α⁡(1/δ))​D/T1−1/α(\sigma_{s}^{2/\alpha-1}\sigma_{l}^{2-2/\alpha}+\sigma_{s}\ln^{1-1/\alpha}(1/\delta))D/T^{1-1/\alpha} for TT oracle calls and failure probability δ\delta, where σs\sigma_{s} and σl\sigma_{l} bound the directional and the full α\alpha-th moment of the noise and DD is the initial distance; in dimension one, where σs=σl\sigma_{s}=\sigma_{l}, this coincides with the dependence on KK, σ0\sigma_{0}, RR, and β\beta in Propositions H.2 and H.3, which are derived for the smooth unconstrained problem and have explicit constants, while the dimension-dependent improvements via σs\sigma_{s} have no counterpart in our setting.

The same construction with a confidence-dependent revelation probability gives the dependence on the confidence level.

ℙ{τ<∞}≤ℙ{supkMk≥1}≤M0≤exp(−κ​λ2​L)=9−1/(2γ¯L)≤13.\mathbb{P}\{\tau<\infty\}\leq\mathbb{P}\left\{\sup_{k}M_{k}\geq 1\right\}\leq M_{0}\leq\exp\left(-\frac{\kappa\lambda}{2L}\right)=9^{-1/(2\bar{\gamma}L)}\leq\frac{1}{3}.

On {τ=∞}\{\tau=\infty\}, we have xk=x0+λ​∑j<kγj​χjx^{k}=x^{0}+\lambda\sum_{j<k}\gamma_{j}\chi_{j} for all kk. Let Γk:=∑j<kγj→∞\Gamma_{k}:=\sum_{j<k}\gamma_{j}\to\infty. Since ∑j≥0γj2/Γj+12≤γ¯​(1γ0+∑j≥1(1Γj−1Γj+1))≤2​γ¯γ0\sum_{j\geq 0}\gamma_{j}^{2}/\Gamma_{j+1}^{2}\leq\bar{\gamma}\left(\frac{1}{\gamma_{0}}+\sum_{j\geq 1}\left(\frac{1}{\Gamma_{j}}-\frac{1}{\Gamma_{j+1}}\right)\right)\leq\frac{2\bar{\gamma}}{\gamma_{0}}, the martingale ∑j<kγj​(χj−0.8)/Γj+1\sum_{j<k}\gamma_{j}(\chi_{j}-0.8)/\Gamma_{j+1} is bounded in L2L^{2} and converges almost surely. By Kronecker’s lemma, 1Γk​∑j<kγj​(χj−0.8)→0\frac{1}{\Gamma_{k}}\sum_{j<k}\gamma_{j}(\chi_{j}-0.8)\to 0; hence, 1Γk​∑j<kγj​χj→0.8\frac{1}{\Gamma_{k}}\sum_{j<k}\gamma_{j}\chi_{j}\to 0.8 and xk→+∞x^{k}\to+\infty almost surely on {τ=∞}\{\tau=\infty\}, which concludes the proof. ∎

Let Assumption 3.1 hold on Q=Bρ​R​(x∗)Q=B_{\rho R}(x^{*}) for some ρ>0\rho>0, and let Assumption 3.4 or Assumption 3.5 hold on QQ. Then 𝟏AX​g​(X,ξ)∈L1\mathbf{1}_{A_{X}}g(X,\xi)\in L^{1} and

𝔼[𝟏AXg(X,ξ)∣𝒢]=𝟏AX∇f(X).\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{1}_{A_{X}}g(X,\xi)\mid\mathcal{G}\right]=\mathbf{1}_{A_{X}}\nabla f(X). (66)

Moreover, almost surely, under Assumption 3.5, for every u>0u>0,

and under Assumption 3.4, 𝟏AX​𝔼​[‖g⁡(X,ξ)−∇f​(X)‖α∣𝒢]≤𝟏AX​(σ0α+σ1α​‖∇f​(X)‖α)\mathbf{1}_{A_{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[\|g(X,\xi)-\nabla f(X)\|^{\alpha}\mid\mathcal{G}\right]\leq\mathbf{1}_{A_{X}}\left(\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}\|\nabla f(X)\|^{\alpha}\right).

Proof.

Since x∗x^{*} is an unconstrained minimizer of the differentiable function ff, we have ∇f​(x∗)=0\nabla f(x^{*})=0, and Assumption 3.1 gives

‖∇f​(x)‖≤L​‖x−x∗‖≤ρ​L​R,x∈Q.\|\nabla f(x)\|\leq L\|x-x^{*}\|\leq\rho LR,\qquad x\in Q. (68)

Let MQ:=(σ0α+σ1α​(ρ​L​R)α)1/αM_{Q}:=(\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}(\rho LR)^{\alpha})^{1/\alpha}. For every x∈Qx\in Q, we have

𝔼ξ​‖g⁡(x,ξ)‖≤ρ​L​R+αα−1​MQ.\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\|g(x,\xi)\|\leq\rho LR+\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}M_{Q}. (69)

Indeed, under Assumption 3.4, this follows from Lyapunov’s inequality, 𝔼ξ​‖g⁡(x,ξ)−∇f​(x)‖≤MQ\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|\leq M_{Q}. Under Assumption 3.5, for Y≥0Y\geq 0 and M>0M>0 with ℙ{Y>u}≤min{1,Mαu−α}\mathbb{P}\{Y>u\}\leq\min\{1,M^{\alpha}u^{-\alpha}\} for all u>0u>0, we have 𝔼​Y≤∫0M⁡𝑑u+Mα​∫M∞u−α​⁡𝑑u=αα−1​M\mathbb{E}Y\leq\int_{0}^{M}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u+M^{\alpha}\int_{M}^{\infty}u^{-\alpha}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}M; for M=0M=0, Y=0Y=0 almost surely.

Next, the vector XQ:=X​𝟏AX+x∗​𝟏AXcX_{Q}:=X\mathbf{1}_{A_{X}}+x^{*}\mathbf{1}_{A_{X}^{c}} is 𝒢\mathcal{G}-measurable and belongs to QQ. By independence and joint measurability, for every jointly measurable φ\varphi with 𝔼​|φ⁡(XQ,ξ)|<∞\mathbb{E}|\varphi(X_{Q},\xi)|<\infty, we have

𝔼⁡[φ⁡(XQ,ξ)∣𝒢]=𝔼ξ∼𝒟​φ​(x,ξ)|x=XQ.\mathbb{E}\left[\varphi(X_{Q},\xi)\mid\mathcal{G}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{D}}\,\varphi(x,\xi)\big|_{x=X_{Q}}.

This formula is verified first for indicators of measurable rectangles in (x,ξ)(x,\xi), then for simple functions, and, finally, for integrable functions by monotone convergence and splitting into positive and negative parts. By (69), g⁡(XQ,ξ)g(X_{Q},\xi) is integrable, uniformly in the value of XQX_{Q}, and 𝔼⁡[g⁡(XQ,ξ)∣𝒢]=∇f​(XQ)\mathbb{E}[g(X_{Q},\xi)\mid\mathcal{G}]=\nabla f(X_{Q}). Multiplying by 𝟏AX\mathbf{1}_{A_{X}}, on which XQ=XX_{Q}=X, we get (66). For the tail indicator φ=𝟏{∥g(x,ξ)−∇f(x)∥>u}\varphi=\mathbf{1}\{\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|>u\} and for the non-negative function φ=‖g⁡(x,ξ)−∇f​(x)‖α\varphi=\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|^{\alpha}, the same formula does not require the integrability of gg. For the tail probabilities, we choose the version supplied by the freezing formula; the pointwise tail assumption then gives the inequality simultaneously for every u>0u>0. Together with Assumption 3.5 (resp. Assumption 3.4), it gives the remaining claims, which concludes the proof. ∎

Without additional integrability of g⁡(X,ξ)g(X,\xi), the conditional expectation 𝔼⁡[g⁡(X,ξ)∣𝒢]\mathbb{E}[g(X,\xi)\mid\mathcal{G}] outside QQ is never used. For example, if g⁡(x,ξ)=xg(x,\xi)=x and XX has a Cauchy distribution, then the vector g⁡(X,ξ)g(X,\xi) is not integrable, while its restriction to {X∈Q}\{X\in Q\} is. In contrast, the clipped oracle is always bounded and has an ordinary conditional expectation on the whole probability space.

I.6.

The crude bound ‖∇f​(xt+1)‖≤2​L​R\|\nabla f(x^{t+1})\|\leq 2LR would give only a budget of the order Rα​Kα+1/aαR^{\alpha}K^{\alpha+1}/a^{\alpha}, while Lemma I.5 gives Rα​K/aα/2R^{\alpha}K/a^{\alpha/2}. I.5 Proof of Theorem I.1

As in the proof of Proposition F.6, our proof is induction-based: by induction, we show that the quantities BtB_{t} and the distances ‖zt−x∗‖\|z^{t}-x^{*}\| remain bounded with high probability.

Step 1: induction events and applicability of the potential.

To formulate the statement rigorously, for k=0,…,Kk=0,\dots,K, we introduce probability event Ek∈𝒢kE_{k}\in\mathcal{G}_{k} as follows: for all 0≤t≤k0\leq t\leq k,

We will prove by induction that ℙ⁡(Ek)≥1−k​β/K\mathbb{P}(E_{k})\geq 1-k\beta/K for all k=0,1,…,Kk=0,1,\dots,K. The base of the induction (k=0k=0) follows from B0=0B_{0}=0 and ‖z0−x∗‖≤R\|z^{0}-x^{*}\|\leq R. I.7 Comparison with a Uniform Noise Scale

Let the assumptions of Theorem I.1 hold and let σ¯:=(σ0α+(3​L​R​σ1)α)1/α\bar{\sigma}:=(\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+(3LR\sigma_{1})^{\alpha})^{1/\alpha}. Moreover, with a:=min⁡{a∗​(K,β),auni}a:=\min\{a_{*}(K,\beta),a_{\rm uni}\}, with probability at least 1−β1-\beta, the localization from Theorem I.1 holds and f⁡(yK)−f∗≤6​L​R2K⁡(K+3)​min⁡{a∗​(K,β),auni}f(y^{K})-f^{*}\leq\frac{6LR^{2}}{K(K+3)}\min\{a_{*}(K,\beta),a_{\rm uni}\}.

Proof.

By (68), we have ‖∇f​(x)‖≤3​L​R\|\nabla f(x)\|\leq 3LR on QQ, and, therefore, σ0α+σ1α​‖∇f​(x)‖α≤σ¯α\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}\|\nabla f(x)\|^{\alpha}\leq\bar{\sigma}^{\alpha} for all x∈Qx\in Q, and both (2) and (3) hold with (σ¯,0)(\bar{\sigma},0). Theorem I.1 with the parameters (σ¯,0)(\bar{\sigma},0) has the threshold aunia_{\rm uni} and gives (85). To prove the last claim, we notice that aa is deterministic. If it equals a∗​(K,β)a_{*}(K,\beta), we apply Theorem I.1 with (σ0,σ1)(\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1}); otherwise, we apply it with (σ¯,0)(\bar{\sigma},0). In both cases, (62) holds with probability at least 1−β1-\beta, and no additional union bound is needed, which concludes the proof. ∎

The factor 33 in σ¯\bar{\sigma} ensures that the tail condition holds on the whole set QQ, on which the assumptions of Theorem I.1 are imposed. Since all queries are localized in B2​R​(x∗)B_{2R}(x^{*}), repeating the probabilistic argument would allow a smaller factor, but this is not needed for the comparison of the orders. Since σ¯≤σ0+3​L​R​σ1\bar{\sigma}\leq\sigma_{0}+3LR\sigma_{1}, the multiplicative part contributes O⁡(σ1​L​R2​(H/K)r)O(\sigma_{1}LR^{2}(H/K)^{r}) to (85). Theorem I.1 replaces this term with σ12​L​R2​(H/K)2​r\sigma_{1}^{2}LR^{2}(H/K)^{2r}. The ratio of the two scales is of the order σ1​(H/K)r\sigma_{1}(H/K)^{r} and tends to zero for fixed σ1\sigma_{1} and β\beta as K→∞K\to\infty; we do not claim that this is a uniform improvement for all KK and σ1\sigma_{1}. For σ0>0\sigma_{0}>0, the overall order may be determined by the additive term σ0​R​(H/K)r\sigma_{0}R(H/K)^{r}, meaning that the improvement of the multiplicative part does not necessarily change the leading power. The comparison concerns the polynomial powers of the horizon; at the weak-L2L^{2} endpoint, both bounds also contain the tail-dependent logarithmic coefficients c0,2,c1,2c_{0,2},c_{1,2} from Theorem I.1.

Comparison with prior analyses.

We emphasize that the polynomial rates themselves are not new: for σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0, the exponents of KK and ε\varepsilon in (63) coincide with the ones from Gorbunov et al., (2020) at α=2\alpha=2 and from Sadiev et al., (2023) for α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2], and, for Clip-SGD, with the ones from Sadiev et al., (2023) (see Table 1). What changes is the setting in which they hold.

First, the noise class: the weak-LαL^{\alpha} condition, and, at α=2\alpha=2, the Lorentz scale, replace the bounded α\alpha-th moment, and, therefore, the rates cover the noise whose α\alpha-th moment is infinite.

Second, the affine structure: the gradient-dependent part of the noise enters only through the terms σ12​L​R2​(H/K)2​r\sigma_{1}^{2}LR^{2}(H/K)^{2r} (Clip-SSTM) and Δ1\Delta_{1} (Clip-SGD), which decay in KK faster than the additive term. Affine noise with finite variance (α=2\alpha=2, σ1>0\sigma_{1}>0) is the classical setting from Bottou et al., (2018); related affine conditions appear in the analyses of adaptive stepsizes by Faw et al., (2022); Wang et al., (2023) (affine conditional variance, non-convex criteria) and Attia and Koren, (2023) (almost surely bounded affine noise in the main condition, with a sub-Gaussian extension). At α=2\alpha=2, our multiplicative term has the order σ12​L​R2/K\sigma_{1}^{2}LR^{2}/K, up to logarithmic factors, which matches the variance term from the finite-variance analyses; the criteria and assumptions differ, meaning that this is a comparison of the orders only.

We do not claim that this term is optimal: we do not provide a lower bound for the multiplicative part, and, under purely multiplicative noise with additional structure, e.g., σ0=0\sigma_{0}=0 and strong convexity, faster guarantees are known (Gower et al.,, 2019).

Faster polynomial decay is also possible without strong convexity under a global strong growth condition: under Assumption 3.4 with α=2\alpha=2 and σ0=0\sigma_{0}=0, unbiasedness gives 𝔼​‖g⁡(x,ξ)‖2=‖∇f​(x)‖2+𝔼​‖g⁡(x,ξ)−∇f​(x)‖2≤(1+σ12)​‖∇f​(x)‖2\mathbb{E}\|g(x,\xi)\|^{2}=\|\nabla f(x)\|^{2}+\mathbb{E}\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|^{2}\leq(1+\sigma_{1}^{2})\|\nabla f(x)\|^{2}, and Vaswani et al., (2019, Theorem 2) derive, for an accelerated method under global smoothness and strong growth with constant ρ=1+σ12\rho=1+\sigma_{1}^{2}, the bound 𝔼​f​(xK)−f∗≤2​ρ2​L​R2/K2\mathbb{E}f(x^{K})-f^{*}\leq 2\rho^{2}LR^{2}/K^{2}; hence, 2​ρ2​L​R2/(β​K2)2\rho^{2}LR^{2}/(\beta K^{2}) with probability at least 1−β1-\beta by Markov’s inequality, which is a faster polynomial order at fixed confidence with a much worse dependence on β\beta than our logarithmic one. Gupta et al., (2024) also obtain acceleration in expectation for smooth convex and strongly convex problems through AGNES, under global multiplicative finite-variance noise and with arbitrary noise-to-gradient ratios. These results concern different algorithms and assumptions and show why our multiplicative term should not be regarded as optimal. An analysis bounding the noise scale uniformly over the ball does not retain the separation of the additive and gradient-dependent components (see Corollary I.9).

Third, localization: the smoothness, convexity, and noise assumptions are imposed only on the ball QQ, and all iterates remain in B2​R​(x∗)B_{2R}(x^{*}) on the high-probability event (in Theorem G.1, up to the first iterate in the neighborhood). Fourth, the guarantees are high-probability ones with logarithmic dependence on 1/β1/\beta and with explicit constants and parameter choices; the logarithmic dependence on the horizon in ℓ\ell and HH is an artifact of the union bound and can be removed outside the Λ\Lambda-dependent weak-case tuning (see Appendix I.9).

An optimization lower bound on the Lorentz scale.

Next, we show that the Lorentz logarithm is necessary for optimization itself, in the additive noise class. The oracle model is the same as in Proposition H.2: the algorithm makes at most KK adaptive, possibly randomized, calls to a stochastic gradient oracle, which returns fresh independent samples at successive calls; query points, the decision to stop, and the output are measurable functions of the known class parameters, the previous responses, and an independent random seed; no exact function values are supplied. For a real random variable YY with law PP, we write ‖Y‖2,s;P\|Y\|_{2,s;P} for the quasi-norm defined above (the rearrangement is taken under PP) and omit PP when it is clear from the context.

Thus, σ0RK−1/2[ln(eK)]1/2−1/s\sigma_{0}RK^{-1/2}[\ln(eK)]^{1/2-1/s} is the asymptotic minimax order over the additive L2,sL^{2,s} class at fixed confidence, and both Clip-SGD and Clip-SSTM attain this order. The asymptotic qualification accounts for the cap L​R2LR^{2} in the lower bound and the deterministic terms in the upper bounds. That is, not all logarithmic factors from the earlier bounds are statistically necessary: the logarithmic dependence on the horizon in ℓ\ell and HH comes from the union bound, while the Lorentz factor has a lower bound of its own. For 1<α<21<\alpha<2, the dependence on β\beta in (91) is optimal as well (see Proposition H.3).

Appendix J Additional Experiments

In this section, we present additional experiments complementing Section 6: an experiment with symmetric noise on a quadratic problem, a ridge regression problem on real data with the asymmetric noise from Section 6, and the experiments with the full theoretical parameter prescriptions from Theorems F.1 and I.1 on a smooth convex benchmark with vanishing curvature. We start with the description of the full experimental protocol.

Protocol.

We use α=3/2\alpha=3/2 and 10241024 independent runs per configuration. The reported horizons reach 10610^{6} oracle calls. For Clip-SGD, we report the mean of f⁡(x¯n−1)−f∗f(\bar{x}^{n-1})-f^{*}, where x¯n−1=n−1​∑k=0n−1xk\bar{x}^{n-1}=n^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}x^{k} is the averaged iterate after nn oracle calls (one call per iteration); for Clip-SSTM, we report the mean of f⁡(yn)−f∗f(y^{n})-f^{*}, using the output prescribed by Algorithm 2, without additional averaging. The bands are pointwise approximate 95%95\% confidence intervals for the mean. Horizon-dependent configurations restart from the same initial point for each terminal horizon; the theoretical failure parameter is β=0.05\beta=0.05.

Let PP satisfy ℙ{P>t}=t−α\mathbb{P}\{P>t\}=t^{-\alpha} for t≥1t\geq 1; then 𝔼​P=3\mathbb{E}P=3 and 𝔼​Pα=∞\mathbb{E}P^{\alpha}=\infty. We use either Z=ϵ​PZ=\epsilon P, with an independent Rademacher sign ϵ\epsilon, or the centered asymmetric Z=(P−3)/2Z=(P-3)/2. Both of them satisfy 𝔼​Z=0\mathbb{E}Z=0 and supu>0uℙ{|Z|>u}1/α≤1\sup_{u>0}u\,\mathbb{P}\{|Z|>u\}^{1/\alpha}\leq 1. In the scalar experiments, g⁡(x)=x+S⁡(x)​Z,S⁡(x)=(σ0α+σ1α​|x|α)1/α.g(x)=x+S(x)Z,\;S(x)=\bigl(\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}|x|^{\alpha}\bigr)^{1/\alpha}. The vector oracles are specified in each experiment. All of them satisfy the affine weak-tail inequality with the stated (σ0,σ1)(\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1}); whenever the noise scale is non-zero, its α\alpha-th moment is infinite.

Small additive noise under symmetric noise.

We minimize f⁡(x)=x2/2f(x)=x^{2}/2 on ℝ\mathbb{R} (L=1L=1, x∗=0x^{*}=0) starting from x0=1x^{0}=1 with the symmetric noise, σ1=0.03\sigma_{1}=0.03, the constant stepsize γ=0.05\gamma=0.05, and the constant clipping level λ=1\lambda=1, and vary σ0∈{0,0.01,0.1,0.5,1}\sigma_{0}\in\{0,0.01,0.1,0.5,1\} (see Figure 2).

For σ0=0\sigma_{0}=0, the noise scale vanishes at x∗x^{*}, and the observed error closely tracks the noiseless reference (γ​n)−2/2(\gamma n)^{-2}/2 over the plotted range. For σ0>0\sigma_{0}>0, the curves leave this reference earlier as σ0\sigma_{0} increases and then decay approximately as 1/n1/n, at levels increasing with σ0\sigma_{0}. The exact noiseless averaged error, when clipping is inactive, is (1−(1−γ)n)2/(2​γ2​n2)(1-(1-\gamma)^{n})^{2}/(2\gamma^{2}n^{2}); the plotted reference is its large-nn limit.

Two features of this example go beyond the tail assumption. For symmetric ZZ and even SS, the mean clipped field mλ​(x):=𝔼​clip​(x+S⁡(x)​Z,λ)m_{\lambda}(x):=\mathbb{E}\texttt{clip}(x+S(x)Z,\lambda) is odd, and, therefore, mλ​(0)=0m_{\lambda}(0)=0; its zero is unique here, although, in general, mλ​(x)≠∇f​(x)m_{\lambda}(x)\neq\nabla f(x) for x≠0x\neq 0: since σ0≤1\sigma_{0}\leq 1 and σ1=0.03\sigma_{1}=0.03, we have S⁡(x)≤σ0+σ1​|x|<1+|x|S(x)\leq\sigma_{0}+\sigma_{1}|x|<1+|x| for x≠0x\neq 0; for x>0x>0 and a≥0a\geq 0, the sum clip​(x+a,1)+clip​(x−a,1)\texttt{clip}(x+a,1)+\texttt{clip}(x-a,1) is non-negative and positive when a<x+1a<x+1, which is provided by the event {S(x)P<x+1}\{S(x)P<x+1\} of positive probability (the case S⁡(x)=0S(x)=0 is immediate); hence, m1​(x)>0m_{1}(x)>0 for x>0x>0 and, by oddness, m1​(x)<0m_{1}(x)<0 for x<0x<0. Thus, clipping does not displace the stationary point in this experiment, and the stepsize is constant rather than tied to the horizon as in Corollary F.5. That is, the experiment illustrates the dependence on σ0\sigma_{0}, through which the additive noise enters both the neighborhood 𝒩λ\mathcal{N}_{\lambda} and the vanishing term 𝒱λ,K\mathcal{V}_{\lambda,K} from Corollary F.5, and not the convergence to x∗x^{*} with a fixed stepsize for arbitrary weak-LαL^{\alpha} noise, which fails in general (see Theorem H.1).

Details of the clipping-level experiment.

In the experiment from Figure 1 (see Section 6), γ∗​(n)=min⁡{γL,γ0,γ1,γ2}\gamma_{*}(n)=\min\{\gamma_{L},\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}\} and ℓn=ln⁡(4​n/β)\ell_{n}=\ln(4n/\beta) are computed for the horizon nn with β=0.05\beta=0.05, which gives λ⁡(102)=2.8\lambda(10^{2})=2.8, λ⁡(104)=32\lambda(10^{4})=32, and λ⁡(106)≈570\lambda(10^{6})\approx 570; each horizon nn is a separate run with λ⁡(n)\lambda(n) being constant within the run. The dotted lines are the values f⁡(xλ)f(x_{\lambda}) at the zero xλx_{\lambda} of the mean clipped field x↦𝔼​clip​(g⁡(x),λ)x\mapsto\mathbb{E}\texttt{clip}(g(x),\lambda), computed numerically; xλ>0x_{\lambda}>0, since clipping cuts the heavy right tail of ZZ. They decrease with λ\lambda roughly as λ−2​(α−1)\lambda^{-2(\alpha-1)}, since, on a quadratic, the error at the biased fixed point is the squared bias divided by 2​L2L, and the bias scales as σ0α/λα−1\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}/\lambda^{\alpha-1} (see Lemma 4.1). The zero xλx_{\lambda} of the mean clipped field is a reference for the observed plateau: with a non-zero constant stepsize, the stochastic iterates may fluctuate around this point, and the limiting error of their average is not necessarily equal to f⁡(xλ)−f∗f(x_{\lambda})-f^{*} exactly.

Regression on real data.

We minimize f⁡(w)=12​m​‖A​w−y‖2+0.012​‖w‖2f(w)=\frac{1}{2m}\|Aw-y\|^{2}+\frac{0.01}{2}\|w\|^{2} on the Diabetes dataset (Efron et al.,, 2004), with standardized features and targets (m=442m=442, d=10d=10; loaded with scikit-learn, Pedregosa et al.,, 2011), starting from w0=0w^{0}=0. Here L=λmax​(∇2f)≈4.0L=\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^{2}f)\approx 4.0 and λmin​(∇2f)≈0.019\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^{2}f)\approx 0.019. We use the same clipping levels as above, with R=‖w0−w∗‖R=\|w^{0}-w^{*}\| and this LL in λ⁡(n)\lambda(n), and the common stepsize γ=0.05/L\gamma=0.05/L (Figure 3).

The oracle is g⁡(w,Z)=∇f​(w)+S⁡(w)​Z​eg(w,Z)=\nabla f(w)+S(w)Ze, where ZZ is the centered asymmetric Pareto variable, (σ0,σ1)=(0.05,0.001)(\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1})=(0.05,0.001), and ee is a fixed unit eigenvector of the smallest Hessian eigenvalue. The projected scale S⁡(w):=(σ0α+σ1α​|⟨∇f​(w),e⟩|α)1/αS(w):=(\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}|\left\langle\nabla f(w),e\right\rangle|^{\alpha})^{1/\alpha} satisfies Assumption 3.5, since |⟨∇f​(w),e⟩|≤‖∇f​(w)‖|\left\langle\nabla f(w),e\right\rangle|\leq\|\nabla f(w)\|. This oracle is also the gradient of f⁡(w)+Z​Ψ​(⟨w−w∗,e⟩)f(w)+Z\Psi(\left\langle w-w^{*},e\right\rangle), with Ψ′​(u)=(σ0α+σ1α​λminα​|u|α)1/α\Psi^{\prime}(u)=(\sigma_{0}^{\alpha}+\sigma_{1}^{\alpha}\lambda_{\min}^{\alpha}|u|^{\alpha})^{1/\alpha}, although our model does not require a sample-objective representation.

For small clipping levels, the error first decreases and then rises toward a plateau. This behavior is consistent with a displacement of the equilibrium of the mean clipped field. If ∇f​(wλ)=b​e\nabla f(w_{\lambda})=be, the quadratic structure gives wλ−w∗=(b/λmin)​ew_{\lambda}-w^{*}=(b/\lambda_{\min})e and f⁡(wλ)−f∗=b2/(2​λmin)f(w_{\lambda})-f^{*}=b^{2}/(2\lambda_{\min}), illustrating how low curvature can amplify clipping bias. Since the experiment uses a positive constant stepsize, this equilibrium value is a reference for the observed plateau, not an exact formula for the limiting error of the averaged iterates. Larger levels lower the observed plateau, and λ⁡(n)\lambda(n) yields decreasing error over the tested horizons.

Relation to the theory.

The clipping level λ⁡(n)\lambda(n) is the one prescribed by Theorem 5.1 for the horizon nn, but the stepsize used is the common empirical value rather than the much smaller γ∗​(n)\gamma_{*}(n), and the constant-level runs use a fixed stepsize instead of the horizon-dependent one from Theorem 5.3; therefore, the comparisons isolate the effect of the clipping level and do not test the high-probability bounds themselves.

For the asymmetric-noise examples, larger clipping levels lower the observed plateaus, while the horizon-dependent level yields decreasing error over the tested horizons. The symmetric-noise example illustrates a different case: clipping preserves the zero of the mean field, and the averaged error continues to decrease with a constant level. These observations are consistent with the mechanisms discussed in Sections 5 and 5.2.

The pointwise 95%95\% intervals quantify uncertainty in the estimated mean across runs; they are not 95%95\% guarantees for the error of an individual run. All experiments use α=3/2\alpha=3/2, so they do not directly test the Lorentz endpoint or compare its two theoretical tunings.

Three noise regimes for Clip-SGD.

We compare (σ0,σ1)=(0,0),(0,0.004),(0.002,0)(\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1})=(0,0),(0,0.004),(0.002,0) on this objective, using the full pair γ∗​(n)\gamma_{*}(n) and λ⁡(n)=R/(40​γ∗​(n)​ln⁡(4​n/β))\lambda(n)=R/(40\gamma_{*}(n)\ln(4n/\beta)) from Theorem F.1, recomputed for each configuration and horizon (see Figure 4). The mean averaged-iterate gaps are close at short horizons and separate as the horizon increases: the noiseless case decreases most rapidly, followed by the multiplicative and then the additive noise. Since the prescribed stepsizes depend on the noise coefficients, this separation reflects both the stochastic perturbations and the corresponding conservative tuning. The comparison illustrates the three noise regimes from Corollary F.2, whose upper bounds have the orders n−1n^{-1}, n−2/3n^{-2/3}, and n−1/3n^{-1/3} up to logarithmic factors. These orders describe theoretical upper bounds and are not claimed to be fitted empirical slopes for this instance.

Sensitivity of Clip-SSTM to the noise.

On the same objective, we use the full prescription from Theorem I.1: a=a∗​(n,β)a=a_{*}(n,\beta) and λk=R/(30​ωk+1​Hn)\lambda_{k}=R/(30\omega_{k+1}H_{n}), where ωk+1=(k+2)/(2​a​L)\omega_{k+1}=(k+2)/(2aL) and Hn=ln⁡(4​n/β)H_{n}=\ln(4n/\beta). We vary σ0∈{0,10−5,10−4,10−3}\sigma_{0}\in\{0,10^{-5},10^{-4},10^{-3}\} with σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0 (see Figure 6), and, separately, σ1∈{0,10−4,3⋅10−4,10−3}\sigma_{1}\in\{0,10^{-4},3\cdot 10^{-4},10^{-3}\} with σ0=0\sigma_{0}=0 (see Figure 6). The two plots share the same noiseless control and cover 103≤n≤10610^{3}\leq n\leq 10^{6} on logarithmic axes. The parameter a∗​(n,β)a_{*}(n,\beta) and the associated clipping schedule are recomputed for each noise level and terminal horizon. At the smallest noise levels, the curves closely follow the noiseless control, while larger coefficients lead to markedly slower observed progress. This separation reflects both the stochastic perturbations and the more conservative theoretical tuning required by larger noise coefficients.

Software and data.

We use the diabetes dataset from Efron et al., (2004), loaded through scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al.,, 2011). The scikit-learn software is distributed under the BSD-3-Clause license. The synthetic problems are fully specified by the formulas above.
